description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Atmosphere and Climatology reference material. Covers all topics: atmosphere composition, structure, insolation, temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds, precipitation, climate classification, monsoon, and cyclones. Verify before formal examination use.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the atmosphere?

options.A: A solid layer of rock surrounding Earth
options.B: The envelope of gases and suspended particles surrounding Earth, held mainly by gravity and rotating with the planet
options.C: A liquid layer covering Earth's surface

questions.explanation: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases and suspended particles surrounding Earth, held mainly by gravity and rotating with the planet. It supplies gases essential for life, moderates temperature, supports weather and climate, and protects the surface from harmful radiation and many small meteoroids.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What percentage of dry, clean air near sea level is nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Approximately 78.08% of dry, clean air near sea level is nitrogen by volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What percentage of dry, clean air near sea level is oxygen?
questions.explanation: Approximately 20.95% of dry, clean air near sea level is oxygen by volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What percentage of dry, clean air near sea level is argon?
questions.explanation: Approximately 0.93% of dry, clean air near sea level is argon by volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate percentage of carbon dioxide in dry, clean air near sea level?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide constitutes about 0.04% of dry, clean air near sea level by volume (roughly 420+ ppm in recent years; varies over time).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a trace gas found in the atmosphere?

options.A: Nitrogen
options.B: Oxygen

questions.explanation: Trace gases include neon, helium, methane, krypton, hydrogen, nitrous oxide and ozone. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are major components, not trace gases.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is water vapour excluded from the usual dry-air percentages?

options.A: It is not part of the atmosphere
options.B: It is highly variable in amount
options.C: It is too heavy to measure
options.D: It only exists in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: Water vapour is variable and is excluded from the usual dry-air percentages. Its amount varies greatly with temperature and location, ranging from near 0–4% by volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is nitrogen important in the atmosphere?

options.A: It supports combustion
options.B: It dilutes oxygen and moderates the intensity of combustion

questions.explanation: Nitrogen dilutes oxygen and moderates the intensity of combustion. It is essential to living organisms but most plants cannot use atmospheric N directly; nitrogen-fixing bacteria, lightning and industrial processes convert it into biologically usable forms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is atmospheric nitrogen made available to plants?

options.A: Through direct absorption from air
options.B: Through nitrogen-fixing bacteria, lightning and industrial processes

questions.explanation: Most plants cannot use atmospheric N directly; nitrogen-fixing bacteria, lightning and industrial processes convert it into biologically usable forms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is oxygen important in the atmosphere?

options.A: It is used in photosynthesis only
options.B: It is required for aerobic respiration and supports combustion

questions.explanation: Oxygen is required for aerobic respiration and supports combustion. Atmospheric oxygen is replenished mainly by photosynthesis and consumed by respiration, decomposition, oxidation and combustion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the main source of replenishment of atmospheric oxygen?

options.A: Volcanic eruptions
options.B: Photosynthesis

questions.explanation: Atmospheric oxygen is replenished mainly by photosynthesis and consumed by respiration, decomposition, oxidation and combustion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the importance of atmospheric carbon dioxide?

options.A: It is used in photosynthesis and absorbs outgoing infrared radiation as a greenhouse gas
options.B: It supports combustion
options.D: It is an inert gas with no biological role

questions.explanation: CO2 is used in photosynthesis and absorbs outgoing infrared radiation, making it a greenhouse gas. Its concentration is small but climatically important; human fossil-fuel use and land-use change have raised its concentration.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is argon?

options.A: A reactive gas essential for life
options.B: An inert noble gas forming about 0.93% of dry air

questions.explanation: Argon is an inert noble gas forming about 0.93% of dry air. It has little direct biological or climatic role compared with greenhouse gases.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is ozone and where is most atmospheric ozone found?

options.A: A compound of oxygen found mainly in the troposphere
options.B: A reactive form of oxygen found mainly in the stratosphere
options.C: An inert gas found mainly in the mesosphere
options.D: A greenhouse gas found mainly in the thermosphere

questions.explanation: Ozone (O3) is a reactive form of oxygen. Most atmospheric ozone is in the stratosphere, where it absorbs ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation; near-surface ozone is an air pollutant and respiratory irritant.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of stratospheric ozone?

options.A: It absorbs ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation
options.B: It absorbs infrared radiation

questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation, protecting organisms from harmful ultraviolet exposure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is water vapour in the atmosphere?

options.A: Water in gaseous form whose amount varies greatly with temperature and location
options.B: A trace gas with constant concentration

questions.explanation: Water vapour is water in gaseous form in the atmosphere. Its amount varies greatly with temperature and location; warm air can contain more water vapour than cold air. It is central to humidity, cloud formation, rainfall and the greenhouse effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are atmospheric dust particles or aerosols?

options.A: Large rocks floating in the atmosphere
options.B: Small suspended solid or liquid particles such as mineral dust, sea salt, smoke, soot, pollen and volcanic ash

questions.explanation: Atmospheric dust particles or aerosols are small suspended solid or liquid particles such as mineral dust, sea salt, smoke, soot, pollen and volcanic ash. They scatter or absorb radiation and can act as cloud-condensation or ice-nucleating particles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major layers of the atmosphere by temperature structure?

options.A: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere
options.B: Ionosphere, ozonosphere, neutrosphere
options.D: Inner core, outer core, mantle, crust

questions.explanation: By temperature structure, the major layers are troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere. The ionosphere is an electrically charged region that overlaps mainly the mesosphere and thermosphere; it is not a separate temperature layer.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is the ionosphere a separate temperature-defined layer of the atmosphere?

options.A: Yes, it is the fourth layer after the mesosphere
options.B: No, it is an electrically charged region that overlaps mainly the mesosphere and thermosphere
options.C: Yes, it is below the troposphere
options.D: No, it is part of the exosphere only

questions.explanation: The ionosphere is an electrically charged region that overlaps mainly the mesosphere and thermosphere; it is not a separate temperature layer.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate altitude range of the troposphere?

options.A: Surface to ~8 km at poles; ~16–18 km near equator; average ~12 km
options.B: ~12 to 50 km

questions.explanation: The troposphere extends from the surface to ~8 km at poles; ~16–18 km near equator; average ~12 km.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which layer contains most water vapour and weather phenomena?

options.A: Stratosphere
options.B: Mesosphere

questions.explanation: The troposphere contains most water vapour and weather. It is the lowest atmospheric layer, extending from the surface to the tropopause.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate altitude range of the stratosphere?

options.A: Surface to ~12 km
options.B: ~12 to 50 km

questions.explanation: The stratosphere extends from about 12 km to 50 km altitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does temperature increase upward in the stratosphere?

options.A: Because of convection
options.B: Because ozone absorbs UV radiation

questions.explanation: Temperature increases upward in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs ultraviolet solar radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate altitude range of the mesosphere?

options.A: Surface to ~12 km
options.B: ~12 to 50 km

questions.explanation: The mesosphere extends from about 50 km to 80–85 km altitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens to meteors in the mesosphere?

options.A: They pass through unaffected
options.B: Many meteors burn up (ablate) in this region

questions.explanation: Many incoming meteoroids ablate in the mesosphere. Temperature decreases with altitude and reaches very low values near the mesopause.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate altitude range of the thermosphere?

options.A: Surface to ~12 km
options.B: ~12 to 50 km

questions.explanation: The thermosphere extends from about 85 km to 500–600+ km (variable). Temperature rises sharply; very thin air; auroras and much ionospheric activity occur here.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does temperature rise markedly with height in the thermosphere?

options.A: Because of ozone absorption
options.B: Because sparse gas molecules absorb high-energy solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation

questions.explanation: In the thermosphere, temperature rises markedly with height because sparse gas molecules absorb high-energy solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation. Despite high kinetic temperatures, the air is extremely thin.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the exosphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer
options.B: The outermost atmospheric region where gas particles are so far apart that collisions are infrequent
options.C: The layer where meteors burn up
options.D: The layer containing the ozone layer

questions.explanation: The exosphere is the outermost atmospheric region, where gas particles are so far apart that collisions are infrequent. It gradually merges with interplanetary space. It begins roughly 500–1,000 km and consists of extremely sparse gases, mainly hydrogen and helium.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the troposphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer extending from the surface to the tropopause
options.B: The layer above the stratosphere
options.C: The outermost layer of the atmosphere

questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer, extending from the surface to the tropopause. It contains most atmospheric mass and nearly all weather-related water vapour. Temperature generally decreases with height at an average environmental lapse rate near 6.5°C per kilometre.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the tropopause?

options.A: The boundary between troposphere and stratosphere
options.B: The boundary between stratosphere and mesosphere
options.C: The boundary between mesosphere and thermosphere
options.D: The boundary between thermosphere and exosphere

questions.explanation: The tropopause is the boundary between troposphere and stratosphere. Its altitude is generally higher in the tropics and lower near the poles; it is not a perfectly level surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the stratosphere?

options.A: The layer above the troposphere extending to about 50 km where temperature increases with height through much of it
options.B: The layer where temperature decreases with height
options.C: The layer where meteors burn up
options.D: The outermost layer of the atmosphere

questions.explanation: The stratosphere is the layer above the troposphere, extending to about 50 km. Temperature increases with height through much of it because ozone absorbs ultraviolet solar radiation. Its stable stratification limits vertical mixing compared with the troposphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the mesosphere?

options.A: The layer above the stratopause, roughly 50–80/85 km, where temperature decreases with altitude
options.B: The layer where temperature increases with altitude

questions.explanation: The mesosphere is the layer above the stratopause, roughly 50–80/85 km. Temperature decreases with altitude and reaches very low values near the mesopause. Many incoming meteoroids ablate in this region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the thermosphere?

options.A: A high-altitude layer where temperature rises markedly with height because sparse gas molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation
options.B: The layer where temperature decreases with height
options.D: The layer containing most water vapour

questions.explanation: The thermosphere is a high-altitude layer in which temperature rises markedly with height because sparse gas molecules absorb high-energy solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation. Despite high kinetic temperatures, the air is extremely thin.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the ionosphere?

options.A: A region of the upper atmosphere containing appreciable concentrations of ions and free electrons produced mainly by solar radiation
options.B: A separate temperature layer below the troposphere
options.C: A layer containing only neutral gases
options.D: The lowest layer of the atmosphere

questions.explanation: The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing appreciable concentrations of ions and free electrons produced mainly by solar radiation. It overlaps parts of the mesosphere and thermosphere and affects radio-wave propagation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the ozone layer?

options.A: A region of relatively high ozone concentration in the stratosphere, mainly around 15–35 km altitude
options.B: A layer in the troposphere

questions.explanation: The ozone layer is a region of relatively high ozone concentration in the stratosphere, mainly around 15–35 km altitude. It absorbs most incoming UV-C and much UV-B, protecting organisms from harmful ultraviolet exposure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What causes ozone depletion?

options.A: Carbon dioxide emissions
options.B: Chlorine- and bromine-containing compounds, notably from older chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons, that release reactive halogens in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: Chlorine- and bromine-containing compounds, notably from older chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons, release reactive halogens in the stratosphere that catalytically destroy ozone. The Montreal Protocol has phased down many ozone-depleting substances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which international agreement has phased down many ozone-depleting substances?

options.A: Kyoto Protocol
options.B: Paris Agreement

questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol has phased down many ozone-depleting substances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is the atmosphere important?

options.A: It provides oxygen and carbon dioxide; regulates Earth's energy balance and temperature; enables weather and the water cycle; protects against harmful UV through ozone; burns up many small meteoroids; distributes heat and moisture; and supports sound transmission and life
options.B: It only provides oxygen

questions.explanation: The atmosphere provides oxygen and carbon dioxide; regulates Earth's energy balance and temperature; enables weather and the water cycle; protects against harmful UV through ozone; burns up many small meteoroids; distributes heat and moisture; and supports sound transmission and life.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do composition and structure of the atmosphere work together?

options.A: Composition determines radiative absorption, chemistry and life-support functions; vertical structure controls temperature, stability, mixing, clouds, weather and upper-atmosphere processes
options.B: They are independent and unrelated
options.D: Composition has no effect on climate

questions.explanation: Composition determines radiative absorption, chemistry and life-support functions; vertical structure controls temperature, stability, mixing, clouds, weather and upper-atmosphere processes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is solar radiation?

options.A: Energy emitted by the Sun in the form of electromagnetic radiation, including visible light, ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths
options.B: Energy emitted by Earth

questions.explanation: Solar radiation is energy emitted by the Sun in the form of electromagnetic radiation, including visible light, ultraviolet and infrared wavelengths.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is insolation?

options.A: Outgoing terrestrial radiation
options.B: Incoming solar radiation received by Earth, usually expressed as energy per unit area over a specified period

questions.explanation: Insolation is incoming solar radiation received by Earth, usually expressed as energy per unit area over a specified period. The amount reaching a surface depends on solar angle, day length, atmospheric transparency, season and latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What factors affect the amount of insolation reaching a surface?

options.A: Solar angle, day length, atmospheric transparency, season and latitude
options.B: Only latitude

questions.explanation: The amount of insolation reaching a surface depends on solar angle, day length, atmospheric transparency, season and latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Earth's heat budget?

options.A: The total amount of heat stored in Earth's core
options.B: The balance between incoming solar energy and outgoing reflected shortwave plus emitted longwave radiation
options.C: The heat generated by volcanic activity
options.D: The heat transferred from the ocean to the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Earth's heat budget is the balance between incoming solar energy and outgoing reflected shortwave plus emitted longwave radiation. Over long periods, global-average incoming and outgoing energy are approximately balanced, although regions and seasons have surpluses and deficits.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens to incoming solar radiation?

options.A: All of it is absorbed by the surface
options.B: Some is reflected by clouds, aerosols, the atmosphere and the surface; some is absorbed by the atmosphere and surface; the absorbed energy is later transferred and emitted as infrared radiation
options.C: All of it is reflected back to space
options.D: It is converted entirely into wind energy

questions.explanation: Some incoming solar radiation is reflected by clouds, aerosols, the atmosphere and the surface; some is absorbed by the atmosphere and surface; the absorbed energy is later transferred and emitted as infrared radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is albedo?

options.A: The fraction or percentage of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface
options.B: The amount of heat absorbed by a surface
options.C: The rate of evaporation from a surface

questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction or percentage of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface. Fresh snow has high albedo; oceans and dark forests generally have lower albedo.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which surface has the highest albedo?

options.A: Ocean
options.B: Dark forest

questions.explanation: Fresh snow has high albedo; oceans and dark forests generally have lower albedo.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is absorption of radiation?

options.A: The conversion of radiation energy into internal energy of matter
options.B: The reflection of radiation from a surface
options.C: The scattering of radiation by particles
options.D: The transmission of radiation through a medium

questions.explanation: Absorption is the conversion of radiation energy into internal energy of matter. Ozone and water vapour absorb selected wavelengths in the atmosphere; land and oceans absorb much incoming sunlight.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is radiation as a heat-transfer process?

options.A: Transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves; it does not require a material medium
options.B: Transfer of heat through direct molecular contact
options.C: Vertical transfer of heat by fluid movement
options.D: Horizontal transfer of heat by wind

questions.explanation: Radiation is transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves; it does not require a material medium. The Sun heats Earth mainly by radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is conduction?

options.A: Transfer of heat through direct molecular contact, from warmer to cooler material
options.B: Transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves
options.C: Vertical transfer of heat by fluid movement
options.D: Horizontal transfer of heat by wind

questions.explanation: Conduction is transfer of heat through direct molecular contact, from warmer to cooler material. It warms air immediately next to the ground but is generally less effective for transferring heat through the atmosphere over large vertical distances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is convection?

options.A: Vertical transfer of heat by the movement of fluid, such as rising warm air and sinking cooler air
options.B: Transfer of heat by direct contact
options.C: Horizontal transfer of heat by wind
options.D: Transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves

questions.explanation: Convection is vertical transfer of heat by the movement of fluid, such as rising warm air and sinking cooler air. It is important in atmospheric instability, thermals, clouds and thunderstorms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is advection?

options.A: Vertical transfer of heat by fluid movement
options.B: Horizontal transfer of heat or other atmospheric properties by wind
options.C: Transfer of heat by direct contact
options.D: Transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves

questions.explanation: Advection is horizontal transfer of heat or other atmospheric properties by wind, such as warm-air advection or cold-air advection.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which heat transfer process warms air immediately next to the ground?

options.A: Radiation
options.B: Conduction

questions.explanation: Conduction warms air immediately next to the ground through direct molecular contact.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?

options.A: The natural warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation
options.B: The cooling of Earth's surface due to reflection of sunlight
options.C: The transfer of heat by conduction from the ground
options.D: The depletion of the ozone layer

questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the natural warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation. The natural greenhouse effect makes Earth much warmer than it would otherwise be; increasing greenhouse-gas concentrations strengthen it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which gases are important greenhouse gases?

options.A: Only carbon dioxide
options.B: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and human-made fluorinated gases

questions.explanation: Important greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and human-made fluorinated gases. Water vapour is the largest natural contributor to the greenhouse effect but mainly acts as a feedback; CO2 and other long-lived gases are major drivers of current human-caused warming.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which gas is the largest natural contributor to the greenhouse effect?

options.A: Carbon dioxide
options.B: Methane

questions.explanation: Water vapour is the largest natural contributor to the greenhouse effect but mainly acts as a feedback; CO2 and other long-lived gases are major drivers of current human-caused warming.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is global warming?

options.A: The long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily caused in the modern era by human emissions of greenhouse gases
options.B: A short-term increase in temperature during summer
options.C: The warming of the ocean only
options.D: The increase in solar radiation output

questions.explanation: Global warming is the long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily caused in the modern era by human emissions of greenhouse gases from fossil-fuel combustion, agriculture, industry and land-use change.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between global warming and climate change?

options.A: Global warming refers specifically to the rise in global mean temperature; climate change includes wider long-term changes such as rainfall patterns, extremes, sea level, snow and ice, and ocean conditions
options.B: They are exactly the same thing
options.C: Climate change refers only to temperature rise
options.D: Global warming refers only to sea-level rise

questions.explanation: Global warming refers specifically to the rise in global mean temperature. Climate change includes wider long-term changes such as rainfall patterns, extremes, sea level, snow and ice, and ocean conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is horizontal distribution of temperature?

options.A: The variation of air or surface temperature with altitude
options.B: The variation of air or surface temperature from place to place at broadly the same altitude, commonly represented by isotherms on maps
options.C: The transfer of heat by wind
options.D: The change of temperature with time

questions.explanation: Horizontal distribution of temperature is the variation of air or surface temperature from place to place at broadly the same altitude, commonly represented by isotherms on maps.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are isotherms?

options.A: Lines joining places with equal temperature at a specified time or for a specified period
options.B: Lines joining places with equal pressure
options.C: Lines joining places with equal rainfall
options.D: Lines joining places with equal wind speed

questions.explanation: Isotherms are lines joining places with equal temperature at a specified time or for a specified period. Their pattern is influenced by latitude, land-sea contrast, ocean currents, winds, relief and season.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What factors influence the pattern of isotherms?

options.A: Only latitude
options.B: Latitude, land-sea contrast, ocean currents, winds, relief and season

questions.explanation: The pattern of isotherms is influenced by latitude, land-sea contrast, ocean currents, winds, relief and season.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is vertical distribution of temperature?

options.A: The variation of temperature from place to place at the same altitude
options.B: The change in atmospheric temperature with altitude
options.C: The change of temperature with season
options.D: The change of temperature with longitude

questions.explanation: Vertical distribution of temperature is the change in atmospheric temperature with altitude. In the troposphere temperature usually decreases upward, but inversions and other departures occur.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the normal or average environmental lapse rate?

options.A: The average rate at which environmental air temperature decreases with altitude in the troposphere, approximately 6.5°C per kilometre globally
options.B: The rate at which an unsaturated rising air parcel cools, about 9.8°C per kilometre
options.C: The rate at which temperature increases with altitude
options.D: The rate of temperature change at the equator only

questions.explanation: The normal or average environmental lapse rate is the average rate at which environmental air temperature decreases with altitude in the troposphere, approximately 6.5°C per kilometre globally. Actual lapse rates vary by time, place and atmospheric conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the dry adiabatic lapse rate?

options.A: The rate at which an unsaturated rising air parcel cools by expansion, about 9.8°C per kilometre
options.B: The average environmental lapse rate of 6.5°C per kilometre
options.C: The rate at which temperature increases with altitude
options.D: The rate of cooling of saturated air

questions.explanation: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is the rate at which an unsaturated rising air parcel cools by expansion, about 9.8°C per kilometre. A saturated parcel cools at a lower, variable moist adiabatic rate because condensation releases latent heat.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does a saturated rising air parcel cool at a lower rate than an unsaturated parcel?

options.A: Because condensation releases latent heat
options.B: Because it expands faster

questions.explanation: A saturated parcel cools at a lower, variable moist adiabatic rate because condensation releases latent heat.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is temperature inversion?

options.A: A condition in which air temperature increases with height through a layer, instead of decreasing
options.B: A condition in which temperature decreases with height
options.C: A condition in which pressure is constant
options.D: A condition in which wind stops everywhere

questions.explanation: Temperature inversion is a condition in which air temperature increases with height through a layer, instead of decreasing. It suppresses vertical mixing and can trap pollutants near the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are common types of temperature inversion?

options.A: Radiation inversion, valley or cold-air-pooling inversion, subsidence inversion and frontal inversion
options.B: Only radiation inversion

questions.explanation: Common types of temperature inversion include radiation inversion on clear, calm nights; valley or cold-air-pooling inversion; subsidence inversion under sinking air in high-pressure systems; and frontal inversion where warm air overrides colder air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What causes radiation inversion?

options.A: Clear, calm nights
options.B: Sinking air in high-pressure systems

questions.explanation: Radiation inversion occurs on clear, calm nights when the ground cools rapidly by radiation, cooling the air immediately above it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What factors affect temperature?

options.A: Latitude and solar angle; altitude; distance from sea; ocean currents; prevailing winds and air masses; cloud cover and humidity; slope/aspect; surface albedo and vegetation; season and day length; and urbanisation
options.B: Only latitude

questions.explanation: Factors affecting temperature include latitude and solar angle; altitude; distance from sea; ocean currents; prevailing winds and air masses; cloud cover and humidity; slope/aspect; surface albedo and vegetation; season and day length; and urbanisation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does temperature generally decrease from equator to poles?

options.A: Because the Sun's rays are more direct and concentrated at low latitudes, while high-latitude rays arrive at a lower angle and pass through more atmosphere, spreading energy over a larger area
options.B: Because the poles are farther from the Sun
options.C: Because the equator has more land
options.D: Because the poles have more clouds

questions.explanation: Temperature generally decreases from equator to poles because the Sun's rays are more direct and concentrated at low latitudes, while high-latitude rays arrive at a lower angle and pass through more atmosphere, spreading energy over a larger area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does altitude affect temperature in the troposphere?

options.A: Temperature generally decreases with altitude because the surface is the main heat source and rising air expands and cools
options.B: Temperature increases with altitude

questions.explanation: In the troposphere temperature generally decreases with altitude because the surface is the main heat source and rising air expands and cools. The average environmental lapse rate is about 6.5°C/km but local conditions vary.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does distance from the sea affect temperature?

options.A: Coastal areas usually have smaller daily and annual temperature ranges, while continental interiors often have larger extremes
options.B: Coastal areas have larger temperature ranges
options.C: Distance from sea has no effect
options.D: Continental interiors have smaller temperature ranges

questions.explanation: Water heats and cools more slowly than land. Coastal areas therefore usually have smaller daily and annual temperature ranges, while continental interiors often have larger extremes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do ocean currents influence temperature?

options.A: Warm currents tend to raise temperatures of adjacent coastal areas; cold currents tend to lower coastal temperatures and may stabilise air or promote fog
options.B: Ocean currents have no effect on temperature

questions.explanation: Warm currents tend to raise temperatures of adjacent coastal areas; cold currents tend to lower coastal temperatures and may stabilise air or promote fog.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why do isotherms bend over continents and oceans?

options.A: Because land heats and cools faster than water; in the Northern Hemisphere, isotherms commonly bend poleward over warm continents in summer and equatorward over cold continents in winter
options.B: Because of the Coriolis force only

questions.explanation: Land heats and cools faster than water. In the Northern Hemisphere, isotherms commonly bend poleward over warm continents in summer and equatorward over cold continents in winter; ocean currents also modify the pattern.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is atmospheric pressure?

options.A: The force per unit area exerted by the weight of the air column above a surface
options.B: The temperature of the air
options.C: The amount of water vapour in the air

questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the weight of the air column above a surface. It decreases with altitude because less air remains above.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?

options.A: Newton
options.B: Pascal (Pa)

questions.explanation: The SI unit is pascal (Pa); meteorology commonly uses hectopascal (hPa), numerically equal to millibar (mb). Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hPa.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the standard sea-level pressure?

options.B: 760 hPa

questions.explanation: Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hPa = 1013.25 mb = 760 mm Hg (approx.).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a barometer?

options.A: An instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure
options.B: An instrument used to measure humidity
options.C: An instrument used to measure wind speed
options.D: An instrument used to measure rainfall

questions.explanation: A barometer is an instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does a mercury barometer work?

options.A: A glass tube closed at one end is filled with mercury and inverted into a mercury reservoir; atmospheric pressure supports a column of mercury whose height indicates pressure
options.B: It uses a sealed flexible metal capsule that expands or contracts
options.C: It measures the speed of falling mercury
options.D: It uses a digital sensor only

questions.explanation: A glass tube closed at one end is filled with mercury and inverted into a mercury reservoir. Atmospheric pressure supports a column of mercury; the column height indicates pressure. Standard sea-level pressure supports about 760 mm of mercury.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an aneroid barometer?

options.A: A barometer using a sealed, partially evacuated flexible metal capsule that expands or contracts as external air pressure changes
options.B: A barometer using a column of mercury
options.C: A barometer using a column of water
options.D: A barometer using a digital sensor only

questions.explanation: An aneroid barometer uses a sealed, partially evacuated flexible metal capsule that expands or contracts as external air pressure changes. Mechanical linkages move a pointer or sensor.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are isobars?

options.A: Lines on a weather map joining places with equal atmospheric pressure at a specified time
options.B: Lines joining places with equal temperature
options.C: Lines joining places with equal rainfall
options.D: Lines joining places with equal wind speed

questions.explanation: Isobars are lines on a weather map joining places with equal atmospheric pressure at a specified time, usually reduced to mean sea level for surface charts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What do closely spaced isobars indicate?

options.A: A steep pressure gradient and usually stronger winds
options.B: A weak pressure gradient and light winds

questions.explanation: Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient and usually stronger winds, all else equal. Widely spaced isobars indicate a weaker pressure gradient.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a high-pressure area or anticyclone?

options.A: A region where pressure is higher than surrounding areas, with air generally diverging outward and sinking from aloft
options.B: A region where pressure is lower than surrounding areas, with air converging and rising

questions.explanation: A high-pressure area or anticyclone is a region where pressure is higher than surrounding areas. Near the surface, air generally diverges outward and sinks from aloft; sinking air often suppresses cloud formation, though weather depends on season and moisture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a low-pressure area or depression?

options.A: A region where pressure is higher than surrounding areas
options.B: A region where pressure is lower than surrounding areas, with air generally converging and rising

questions.explanation: A low-pressure area or depression is a region where pressure is lower than surrounding areas. Near the surface, air generally converges and rises, favouring cloud formation and precipitation if moisture and instability are present.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What causes the equatorial low-pressure belt?

options.A: Strong solar heating warms air, which rises in a broad zone near the thermal equator; convergence of trade winds in the ITCZ reinforces the low-pressure belt
options.B: Cold descending air

questions.explanation: Strong solar heating warms air, which rises in a broad zone near the thermal equator. Convergence of trade winds in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) reinforces the low-pressure belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the subtropical high-pressure belt?

options.A: A belt of high pressure near 25°–35° latitude in both hemispheres, associated with descending branches of the Hadley circulation
options.B: A belt of low pressure near the equator
options.C: A belt of low pressure near 50°–70° latitude
options.D: A high-pressure region near the poles

questions.explanation: The subtropical high-pressure belt is a belt of high pressure near 25°–35° latitude in both hemispheres, associated with descending branches of the Hadley circulation. It is often called the horse-latitude belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is another name for the subtropical high-pressure belt?

options.A: Horse-latitude belt
options.B: Doldrums

questions.explanation: The subtropical high-pressure belt is often called the horse-latitude belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What causes the subpolar low-pressure belt?

options.A: Near 50°–70° latitude, relatively warm westerlies meet cold polar easterlies along the polar front; convergence and rising air help form a belt of low pressure, especially over oceans
options.B: Strong solar heating near the equator
options.C: Descending air from the Hadley circulation
options.D: Cold dense air near the poles

questions.explanation: Near 50°–70° latitude, relatively warm westerlies meet cold polar easterlies along the polar front. Convergence and rising air help form a belt of low pressure, especially over oceans.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the polar high-pressure belt?

options.A: A high-pressure region near the poles, associated with very cold, dense air and subsidence
options.B: A low-pressure region near the poles
options.C: A high-pressure region near the equator

questions.explanation: The polar high-pressure belt is a high-pressure region near the poles, associated with very cold, dense air and subsidence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are pressure belts not fixed at exact latitudes?

options.A: They shift seasonally with the apparent movement of the Sun and the thermal equator, and are modified by continents, oceans, topography and seasonal heating
options.B: They are fixed permanently
options.C: They only shift due to ocean currents
options.D: They only shift due to volcanic activity

questions.explanation: Pressure belts are not fixed at exact latitudes because they shift seasonally with the apparent movement of the Sun and the thermal equator, and are modified by continents, oceans, topography and seasonal heating.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are seasonal pressure variations?

options.A: Changes in pressure patterns through the year caused by differential heating of land and sea and seasonal migration of global circulation belts
options.B: Permanent pressure patterns that never change
options.D: Changes caused only by volcanic eruptions

questions.explanation: Seasonal pressure variations are changes in pressure patterns through the year caused by differential heating of land and sea and seasonal migration of global circulation belts. Strong summer heating over Asia produces low pressure that helps draw in moist monsoon air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the pressure gradient force?

options.A: The force arising from differences in pressure over distance; it accelerates air from high towards low pressure
options.B: The force caused by Earth's rotation
options.D: The force caused by gravity only

questions.explanation: The pressure gradient force arises from differences in pressure over distance; it accelerates air from high towards low pressure, though Earth's rotation and friction modify the resulting wind.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is wind?

options.A: The horizontal movement of air relative to Earth's surface, primarily driven by pressure differences
options.B: The vertical movement of air only
options.C: The movement of water in the ocean

questions.explanation: Wind is the horizontal movement of air relative to Earth's surface, primarily driven by pressure differences. Its direction and speed are modified by the Coriolis force, friction and local terrain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are winds classified geographically?

options.A: Planetary or permanent winds; periodic or seasonal winds; and local winds
options.B: Only by speed

questions.explanation: Winds are broadly classified geographically as planetary or permanent winds; periodic or seasonal winds; and local winds. Synoptic-scale winds also include cyclonic and anticyclonic circulations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are planetary winds?

options.A: Large-scale prevailing winds associated with global pressure belts and atmospheric circulation: trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies
options.B: Local winds caused by terrain

questions.explanation: Planetary winds are large-scale prevailing winds associated with global pressure belts and atmospheric circulation: trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are trade winds?

options.A: Persistent easterly winds blowing from subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low; they blow from northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere
options.B: Prevailing westerly winds in middle latitudes
options.C: Cold easterly winds from polar regions

questions.explanation: Trade winds are persistent easterly winds blowing from subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low. They blow from northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are westerlies?

options.A: Prevailing winds flowing from subtropical highs towards subpolar lows, generally from west to east in the middle latitudes
options.B: Easterly winds in the tropics
options.C: Cold easterly winds from polar regions

questions.explanation: Westerlies are prevailing winds flowing from subtropical highs towards subpolar lows, generally from west to east in the middle latitudes. They are often stronger and more variable in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are polar easterlies?

options.A: Cold, generally dry easterly winds flowing outward from polar high-pressure areas towards subpolar low-pressure regions
options.B: Warm, moist westerly winds in middle latitudes

questions.explanation: Polar easterlies are cold, generally dry easterly winds flowing outward from polar high-pressure areas towards subpolar low-pressure regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are periodic winds?

options.A: Winds that reverse or change direction at regular intervals, such as monsoon winds, land and sea breezes, and mountain and valley breezes
options.B: Winds that blow constantly in one direction

questions.explanation: Periodic winds are winds that reverse or change direction at regular intervals, such as monsoon winds (seasonal), land and sea breezes (daily), and mountain and valley breezes (daily).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a monsoon wind?

options.A: A seasonally reversing wind system associated with seasonal differences in heating and pressure between land and ocean, modified by topography, large-scale circulation and ocean-atmosphere interactions
options.B: A daily reversing wind system
options.D: A local wind caused by terrain only

questions.explanation: A monsoon wind is a seasonally reversing wind system associated with seasonal differences in heating and pressure between land and ocean, modified by topography, large-scale circulation and ocean-atmosphere interactions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a sea breeze?

options.A: A daytime coastal wind blowing from sea to land because land heats faster than the sea, creating relatively lower pressure over land
options.B: A nighttime coastal wind blowing from land to sea

questions.explanation: A sea breeze is a daytime coastal wind blowing from sea to land because land heats faster than the sea, creating relatively lower pressure over land.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a land breeze?

options.A: A daytime coastal wind blowing from sea to land
options.B: A nighttime coastal wind blowing from land to sea because land cools faster than the sea, creating relatively higher pressure over land

questions.explanation: A land breeze is a nighttime coastal wind blowing from land to sea because land cools faster than the sea, creating relatively higher pressure over land.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a valley breeze?

options.A: A daytime upslope wind caused by heating of mountain slopes and adjacent air, which rises and draws air up-valley
options.B: A nighttime downslope flow of cooled, dense air

questions.explanation: A valley breeze is a daytime upslope wind caused by heating of mountain slopes and adjacent air, which rises and draws air up-valley.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a mountain breeze?

options.A: A daytime upslope wind
options.B: A nighttime downslope flow of cooled, dense air from mountain slopes into valleys

questions.explanation: A mountain breeze is a nighttime downslope flow of cooled, dense air from mountain slopes into valleys.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Loo?

options.A: A hot, dry summer wind over northwestern and northern India, especially the Indo-Gangetic plain
options.B: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.C: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Loo is a hot, dry summer wind over northwestern and northern India, especially the Indo-Gangetic plain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Chinook?

options.A: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.B: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains in North America that can rapidly raise temperature
options.C: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Chinook is a warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains in North America; it can rapidly raise temperature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Foehn or Föhn?

options.A: A warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of the Alps, similar to Chinook
options.B: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.C: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Foehn or Föhn is a warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of the Alps; similar to Chinook.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Mistral?

options.A: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.B: A cold, strong northerly or northwesterly wind channelled down the Rhône Valley towards the Gulf of Lion
options.C: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Mistral is a cold, strong northerly or northwesterly wind channelled down the Rhône Valley towards the Gulf of Lion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Sirocco?

options.A: A hot, often dusty wind originating over the Sahara and moving towards the Mediterranean; may become humid over the sea
options.B: A cold, gusty downslope wind along the Adriatic coast
options.C: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Sirocco is a hot, often dusty wind originating over the Sahara and moving towards the Mediterranean; it may become humid over the sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Harmattan?

options.A: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.B: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa, especially in boreal winter
options.C: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.D: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains

questions.explanation: The Harmattan is a dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa, especially in boreal winter.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Bora?

options.A: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.B: A cold, gusty downslope wind along the Adriatic coast, especially near the eastern Adriatic
options.C: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Bora is a cold, gusty downslope wind along the Adriatic coast, especially near the eastern Adriatic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are local winds?

options.A: Winds affecting limited regions, often produced by local pressure and temperature contrasts or terrain
options.B: Winds that blow across the entire globe
options.C: Winds that blow only at the equator
options.D: Winds that blow only at the poles

questions.explanation: Local winds are winds affecting limited regions, often produced by local pressure and temperature contrasts or terrain. Their names and effects vary geographically.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Coriolis force?

options.A: An apparent deflection of moving air and water caused by Earth's rotation; it deflects motion to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
options.B: A force caused by pressure differences
options.D: A force caused by gravity only

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is an apparent deflection of moving air and water caused by Earth's rotation. It deflects motion to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere; it is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles. It changes direction, not speed directly.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which direction does the Coriolis force deflect moving air in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.A: To the left
options.B: To the right

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force deflects motion to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Coriolis force zero?

options.A: At the poles
options.B: At the equator

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does the Coriolis force change the speed of wind directly?

options.A: Yes, it increases wind speed
options.B: Yes, it decreases wind speed
options.C: No, it changes direction, not speed directly
options.D: Yes, it both increases and decreases speed

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force changes direction, not speed directly.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are jet streams?

options.A: Narrow bands of very strong winds near the tropopause, generally flowing west to east
options.B: Wide bands of light winds near the surface

questions.explanation: Jet streams are narrow bands of very strong winds near the tropopause, generally flowing west to east. Major types include polar-front and subtropical jet streams; their position and strength vary seasonally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major types of jet streams?

options.A: Polar-front and subtropical jet streams
options.B: Equatorial and polar jet streams only
options.C: Monsoon and trade wind jet streams
options.D: Land and sea breeze jet streams

questions.explanation: Major types include polar-front and subtropical jet streams; their position and strength vary seasonally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do jet streams influence the Indian monsoon?

options.A: Jet streams steer weather systems and influence upper-air divergence and circulation; seasonal shifts, including the northward movement of the subtropical westerly jet and establishment of the tropical easterly jet, are associated with the seasonal evolution of the Indian monsoon
options.B: Jet streams have no influence on the monsoon
options.C: Jet streams only affect winter weather
options.D: Jet streams only affect ocean currents

questions.explanation: Jet streams steer weather systems and influence upper-air divergence and circulation. Seasonal shifts, including the northward movement of the subtropical westerly jet and establishment of the tropical easterly jet, are associated with the seasonal evolution of the Indian monsoon.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are Rossby waves?

options.A: Large-scale meanders in the westerly flow of the atmosphere, caused by the variation of the Coriolis parameter with latitude and influenced by topography and temperature contrasts
options.B: Small-scale waves in the ocean
options.D: Waves in the trade winds only

questions.explanation: Rossby waves are large-scale meanders in the westerly flow of the atmosphere, caused by the variation of the Coriolis parameter with latitude and influenced by topography and temperature contrasts. They help steer weather systems and can produce persistent weather patterns.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an air mass?

options.A: A large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity over a broad horizontal area, acquired from its source region
options.B: A small pocket of air near the ground
options.D: A region of high pressure only

questions.explanation: An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity over a broad horizontal area, acquired from its source region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are air masses classified?

options.A: By moisture source: continental (c, relatively dry) or maritime (m, moist); and by thermal character/latitude: Arctic or Antarctic (A/AA), polar (P) and tropical (T)
options.B: Only by temperature

questions.explanation: Air masses are classified by moisture source: continental (c, relatively dry) or maritime (m, moist); and by thermal character/latitude: Arctic or Antarctic (A/AA), polar (P) and tropical (T). Combined labels include cP, mP, cT and mT.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a front?

options.A: A boundary or transition zone separating air masses with contrasting temperature and density
options.B: A type of cloud

questions.explanation: A front is a boundary or transition zone separating air masses with contrasting temperature and density. Weather changes often occur along fronts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a warm front?

options.A: A front where advancing warm air rises gradually over retreating cold air, commonly producing widespread layered clouds and steady precipitation ahead of the surface front
options.B: A front where advancing cold air undercuts warm air
options.C: A front formed when a cold front catches up with a warm front
options.D: A boundary between two air masses of the same temperature

questions.explanation: A warm front is a front where advancing warm air rises gradually over retreating cold air. It commonly produces widespread layered clouds and steady precipitation ahead of the surface front.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a cold front?

options.A: A front where advancing warm air rises over cold air
options.B: A front where advancing cold, dense air undercuts warm air and forces it to rise more steeply, potentially producing showers, thunderstorms and a relatively abrupt temperature change
options.C: A front formed when a cold front catches up with a warm front
options.D: A boundary between two air masses of the same temperature

questions.explanation: A cold front is a front where advancing cold, dense air undercuts warm air and forces it to rise more steeply. It may produce showers, thunderstorms and a relatively abrupt temperature change.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an occluded front?

options.A: A front where advancing warm air rises over cold air
options.B: A front where advancing cold air undercuts warm air
options.C: A front formed when a faster-moving cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm air off the ground
options.D: A boundary between two air masses of the same temperature

questions.explanation: An occluded front is a front formed when a faster-moving cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm air off the ground. It is commonly associated with a mature mid-latitude cyclone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does a warm front differ from a cold front?

options.A: Warm fronts usually have a gentler slope and broader, steadier precipitation; cold fronts are steeper and may bring narrower bands of intense showers or thunderstorms
options.B: Warm fronts are steeper and bring intense showers
options.C: Cold fronts have a gentler slope and broader precipitation
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: Warm fronts usually have a gentler slope and broader, steadier precipitation; cold fronts are steeper and may bring narrower bands of intense showers or thunderstorms. Actual weather varies.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is friction's role in wind?

options.A: Friction slows wind near the surface and reduces the Coriolis deflection, causing surface winds to cross isobars towards lower pressure; friction decreases with height
options.B: Friction increases wind speed near the surface
options.C: Friction has no effect on wind
options.D: Friction only affects wind at high altitudes

questions.explanation: Friction slows wind near the surface and reduces the Coriolis deflection, causing surface winds to cross isobars towards lower pressure. Friction decreases with height.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is humidity?

options.A: The amount of water vapour present in the air
options.B: The amount of oxygen present in the air

questions.explanation: Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in the air. It may be expressed as absolute humidity, specific humidity, mixing ratio or relative humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is absolute humidity?

options.A: The mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, commonly expressed in grams per cubic metre (g/m³)
options.B: The mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air
options.C: The ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, commonly expressed in grams per cubic metre (g/m³). It changes when air volume changes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is specific humidity?

options.A: The mass of water vapour per unit volume of air
options.B: The mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air, usually expressed in grams per kilogram (g/kg)
options.C: The ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Specific humidity is the mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air, usually expressed in grams per kilogram (g/kg). It is useful because it is less affected by changes in air volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is relative humidity?

options.A: The mass of water vapour per unit volume of air
options.B: The mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air
options.C: The ratio of actual water-vapour pressure to saturation water-vapour pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water-vapour pressure to saturation water-vapour pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage. It depends strongly on temperature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is dew point?

options.A: The temperature to which air must be cooled, at approximately constant pressure and water-vapour content, for it to become saturated
options.B: The temperature at which water freezes
options.C: The temperature at which water boils
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes unsaturated

questions.explanation: Dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, at approximately constant pressure and water-vapour content, for it to become saturated. Dew point is a useful indicator of actual atmospheric moisture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is saturation?

options.A: A state in which air contains the maximum water vapour possible at a given temperature and pressure, so relative humidity is approximately 100%
options.B: A state in which air contains no water vapour
options.C: A state in which air is unsaturated
options.D: A state in which air is frozen

questions.explanation: Saturation is a state in which air contains the maximum water vapour possible at a given temperature and pressure, so relative humidity is approximately 100%.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is evaporation?

options.A: The change of liquid water into water vapour from a surface; it consumes latent heat and is promoted by warmth, wind and low humidity
options.B: The change of water vapour into liquid water
options.C: The change of ice into water
options.D: The change of water into ice

questions.explanation: Evaporation is the change of liquid water into water vapour from a surface. It consumes latent heat and is promoted by warmth, wind and low humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is condensation?

options.A: The change of liquid water into water vapour
options.B: The change of water vapour into liquid water when air reaches saturation and vapour condenses on suitable surfaces or particles; it releases latent heat
options.C: The change of ice into water
options.D: The change of water into ice

questions.explanation: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid water when air reaches saturation and vapour condenses on suitable surfaces or particles. It releases latent heat.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of condensation nuclei?

options.A: Tiny particles such as sea salt, dust and aerosols provide surfaces on which water vapour can condense to form cloud droplets
options.B: They absorb sunlight
options.C: They increase the temperature of the air
options.D: They decrease the humidity of the air

questions.explanation: Tiny particles such as sea salt, dust and aerosols provide surfaces on which water vapour can condense to form cloud droplets. Ice-nucleating particles help ice crystals form.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do clouds form?

options.A: Moist air cools to its dew point, commonly through uplift and expansion, and becomes saturated; water vapour condenses onto cloud-condensation nuclei or deposits as ice crystals, forming visible droplets or crystals
options.B: Dust particles combine to form clouds
options.C: Water vapour rises directly as liquid

questions.explanation: Moist air cools to its dew point, commonly through uplift and expansion, and becomes saturated. Water vapour condenses onto cloud-condensation nuclei or deposits as ice crystals, forming visible droplets or crystals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the four basic cloud-form names?

options.A: Cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus
options.B: Cirrus, altus, stratus and nimbus

questions.explanation: The four basic cloud-form names are cirrus (fibrous/high), cumulus (heap-like), stratus (layer-like) and nimbus (rain-bearing). These combining forms create many cloud genera, such as cumulonimbus and nimbostratus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are cirrus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds; often fair at present, increasing cirrus can precede a change
options.B: Heap-shaped clouds with flat bases

questions.explanation: Cirrus (Ci) clouds are high, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds. Often fair at present; increasing cirrus can precede a change.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are cumulus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Heap-shaped clouds with flat bases; usually low to middle levels; fair-weather cumulus if small, may grow into showers

questions.explanation: Cumulus (Cu) clouds are heap-shaped clouds with flat bases, usually at low to middle levels. Fair-weather cumulus if small; may grow into showers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are stratus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Heap-shaped clouds with flat bases
options.C: Uniform low grey layers; overcast skies, drizzle or mist-like conditions

questions.explanation: Stratus (St) clouds are uniform low grey layers. They produce overcast skies, drizzle or mist-like conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does the term 'nimbus' indicate in cloud names?

options.A: High altitude
options.B: Rain-bearing

questions.explanation: Nimbus is a rain-bearing descriptor, not a standalone modern cloud genus. It is used in names such as nimbostratus and cumulonimbus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are cumulonimbus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Heap-shaped fair-weather clouds
options.D: Deep, vertically developed thunderstorm clouds associated with heavy showers, lightning, hail, gusts and sometimes severe weather

questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus (Cb) clouds are deep, vertically developed thunderstorm clouds. They are associated with heavy showers, lightning, hail, gusts and sometimes severe weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are nimbostratus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Thick, widespread layered clouds producing persistent, widespread rain or snow

questions.explanation: Nimbostratus (Ns) clouds are thick, widespread layered clouds. They produce persistent, widespread rain or snow.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are clouds classified by height and form?

options.A: The World Meteorological Organization recognises ten principal cloud genera, commonly grouped as high clouds, middle clouds, low clouds and clouds with vertical development
options.B: Clouds are classified only by color
options.C: Clouds are classified only by temperature
options.D: Clouds are classified only by wind speed

questions.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization recognises ten principal cloud genera, commonly grouped as high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus), middle clouds (altostratus, altocumulus), low clouds (stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus) and clouds with vertical development (cumulus and cumulonimbus). Height boundaries vary with latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as high clouds?

options.A: Cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: High clouds include cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as middle clouds?

options.A: Cirrus and cirrostratus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: Middle clouds include altostratus and altocumulus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as low clouds?

options.A: Cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: Low clouds include stratus, stratocumulus and nimbostratus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as clouds with vertical development?

options.A: Cirrus and cirrostratus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: Clouds with vertical development include cumulus and cumulonimbus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is fog?

options.A: A cloud at or very near the ground that reduces horizontal visibility, conventionally to less than 1 km in meteorological reporting
options.B: A cloud high in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: Fog is a cloud at or very near the ground that reduces horizontal visibility, conventionally to less than 1 km in meteorological reporting.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is mist?

options.A: A cloud at high altitude
options.B: A suspension of tiny water droplets near the ground that reduces visibility, but generally less severely than fog; a common convention is visibility of 1 km or more

questions.explanation: Mist is a suspension of tiny water droplets near the ground that reduces visibility, but generally less severely than fog; a common convention is visibility of 1 km or more.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is dew?

options.A: Liquid water droplets formed when a surface cools to or below the dew point and water vapour condenses on it
options.B: Ice crystals formed by deposition of water vapour

questions.explanation: Dew is liquid water droplets formed when a surface cools to or below the dew point and water vapour condenses on it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is frost?

options.A: Liquid water droplets formed by condensation
options.B: Ice crystals formed by deposition of water vapour or freezing of dew when it is sufficiently cold

questions.explanation: Frost is ice crystals formed by deposition of water vapour or freezing of dew when it is sufficiently cold.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is hail?

options.A: Balls or irregular lumps of ice produced in strong cumulonimbus updrafts, where ice particles grow by collecting supercooled water droplets before falling
options.B: Small ice pellets formed when raindrops refreeze
options.C: Ice crystals that form on surfaces

questions.explanation: Hail is balls or irregular lumps of ice produced in strong cumulonimbus updrafts, where ice particles grow by collecting supercooled water droplets before falling.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is hail different from sleet?

options.A: Hail grows in strong thunderstorm updrafts and can become large; sleet is generally small ice pellets formed when raindrops or partially melted snow refreeze before reaching the ground
options.B: Hail is small ice pellets; sleet is large ice balls
options.C: Hail and sleet are the same thing
options.D: Hail forms on surfaces; sleet falls from clouds

questions.explanation: Hail grows in strong thunderstorm updrafts and can become large; sleet is generally small ice pellets formed when raindrops or partially melted snow refreeze before reaching the ground. Usage of 'sleet' differs between regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is latent heat?

options.A: Energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature
options.B: Heat transferred by conduction

questions.explanation: Latent heat is energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature. Evaporation absorbs latent heat; condensation, freezing and deposition release it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does relative humidity rise when air cools without adding water vapour?

options.A: Because saturation vapour pressure decreases as temperature falls, so the same actual vapour content becomes a larger fraction of saturation
options.B: Because water vapour is added to the air

questions.explanation: Saturation vapour pressure decreases as temperature falls. The same actual vapour content therefore becomes a larger fraction of saturation, raising relative humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is precipitation?

options.A: Any form of water, liquid or solid, falling from clouds or the atmosphere to Earth's surface, including rain, drizzle, snow, sleet and hail
options.B: Only rainfall

questions.explanation: Precipitation is any form of water, liquid or solid, falling from clouds or the atmosphere to Earth's surface, including rain, drizzle, snow, sleet and hail. Dew and frost form on surfaces and are not precipitation in the strict meteorological sense.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are dew and frost considered precipitation in the strict meteorological sense?

options.A: Yes, they are precipitation
options.B: No, they form on surfaces and are not precipitation in the strict meteorological sense

questions.explanation: Dew and frost form on surfaces and are not precipitation in the strict meteorological sense.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is rainfall?

options.A: Liquid precipitation consisting of water droplets that fall from clouds and reach the ground
options.B: Solid precipitation only

questions.explanation: Rainfall is liquid precipitation consisting of water droplets that fall from clouds and reach the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is convectional rainfall?

options.A: Rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise, expand and cool adiabatically, reach saturation and form clouds, often cumulonimbus; commonly produces intense, short-duration showers and thunderstorms
options.B: Rain produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier
options.C: Precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise, expand and cool adiabatically, reach saturation and form clouds, often cumulonimbus. It commonly produces intense, short-duration showers and thunderstorms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is convectional rainfall common?

options.A: Equatorial regions, tropical interiors and warm-season continental areas where surface heating and moisture are strong
options.B: Polar regions only

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is common in equatorial regions, tropical interiors and warm-season continental areas where surface heating and moisture are strong.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is orographic rainfall?

options.A: Rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise
