options.B: Rainfall produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier; it cools, condenses and precipitates on the windward slope, creating a rain-shadow effect on the leeward side
options.C: Precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts

questions.explanation: Orographic rainfall is rainfall produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier. It cools, condenses and precipitates on the windward slope; descending air on the leeward side becomes warmer and drier, creating a rain-shadow effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is another name for orographic rainfall?

options.A: Convectional rainfall
options.B: Cyclonic rainfall

questions.explanation: Relief rainfall is another name for orographic rainfall, emphasising the role of topography or relief in forcing air upward.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is cyclonic or frontal rainfall?

options.A: Rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise
options.B: Rainfall produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier
options.C: Precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts, where converging air rises; occurs in tropical cyclones and in temperate depressions along warm, cold and occluded fronts

questions.explanation: Cyclonic or frontal rainfall is precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts, where converging air rises. It occurs in tropical cyclones and in temperate depressions along warm, cold and occluded fronts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Differentiate convectional, orographic and cyclonic rainfall.

options.A: Convectional rainfall is driven by surface heating and buoyant uplift; orographic rainfall by forced uplift over mountains; cyclonic/frontal rainfall by convergence and uplift in low-pressure systems or along fronts
options.B: All three types are caused by the same mechanism
options.C: Convectional rainfall is caused by mountains; orographic by fronts; cyclonic by heating
options.D: Convectional rainfall occurs only in winter; orographic only in summer; cyclonic only in spring

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is driven by surface heating and buoyant uplift; orographic rainfall by forced uplift over mountains; cyclonic/frontal rainfall by convergence and uplift in low-pressure systems or along fronts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of rainfall is characterised by intense, localised showers and often thunderstorm activity?

options.A: Orographic rainfall
options.B: Cyclonic rainfall

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is characterised by intense, localised showers and often thunderstorm activity due to surface heating and buoyant rising air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of rainfall produces windward rain and a leeward rain shadow?

options.A: Convectional rainfall
options.B: Orographic or relief rainfall

questions.explanation: Orographic or relief rainfall produces windward rain and a leeward rain shadow.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of rainfall is typically widespread and often longer-lasting?

options.A: Convectional rainfall
options.B: Orographic rainfall

questions.explanation: Cyclonic or frontal rainfall is typically widespread and often longer-lasting due to convergence and frontal overrunning.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is snowfall?

options.A: Precipitation in the form of ice crystals or snowflakes that reach the ground without melting completely; requires a sufficiently cold atmospheric column and surface conditions
options.B: Rain that freezes after hitting the ground
options.C: Ice pellets formed when raindrops refreeze

questions.explanation: Snowfall is precipitation in the form of ice crystals or snowflakes that reach the ground without melting completely. It requires a sufficiently cold atmospheric column and surface conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is sleet?

options.A: Large ice balls produced in thunderstorm updrafts
options.B: A term with regional differences; in many meteorological contexts it refers to small ice pellets formed when melted or partially melted snow refreezes in a subfreezing layer near the ground

questions.explanation: Sleet is a term with regional differences. In many meteorological contexts it refers to small ice pellets formed when melted or partially melted snow refreezes in a subfreezing layer near the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are hailstorms?

options.A: Thunderstorms that produce hailstones, which grow in strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds by accretion of supercooled water
options.B: Storms that produce only rain

questions.explanation: Hailstorms are thunderstorms that produce hailstones, which grow in strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds by accretion of supercooled water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is precipitation measured?

options.A: Rainfall is measured using rain gauges, commonly reported in millimetres (mm), where 1 mm of rainfall equals 1 litre of water per square metre on a level surface, assuming no losses
options.B: Rainfall is measured using a barometer
options.C: Rainfall is measured using a thermometer
options.D: Rainfall is measured using an anemometer

questions.explanation: Rainfall is measured using rain gauges, commonly reported in millimetres (mm), where 1 mm of rainfall equals 1 litre of water per square metre on a level surface, assuming no losses.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a rain gauge?

options.A: An instrument that collects and measures liquid precipitation over a known area
options.B: An instrument that measures atmospheric pressure
options.C: An instrument that measures wind speed

questions.explanation: A rain gauge is an instrument that collects and measures liquid precipitation over a known area. Standard gauges may be non-recording or recording; tipping-bucket and weighing gauges provide time-resolved measurements.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an isohyet?

options.A: A line on a map joining places with equal temperature
options.B: A line on a map joining places with equal pressure
options.C: A line on a map joining places receiving equal amounts of precipitation over a specified period
options.D: A line on a map joining places with equal wind speed

questions.explanation: An isohyet is a line on a map joining places receiving equal amounts of precipitation over a specified period.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What factors affect rainfall distribution?

options.A: Latitude and global circulation; prevailing winds and moisture sources; distance from sea; mountain barriers and aspect; ocean currents; temperature and evaporation; air-mass and frontal activity; monsoon systems; and seasonal shifts of pressure belts
options.B: Only latitude

questions.explanation: Factors affecting rainfall distribution include latitude and global circulation; prevailing winds and moisture sources; distance from sea; mountain barriers and aspect; ocean currents; temperature and evaporation; air-mass and frontal activity; monsoon systems; and seasonal shifts of pressure belts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does the windward side of a mountain receive more rain?

options.A: Moist air is forced to rise, cool and condense on the windward slope; after losing moisture, descending air on the leeward side warms and its relative humidity decreases, reducing rainfall
options.B: The windward side is closer to the sun
options.C: The windward side has more vegetation
options.D: The windward side has higher pressure

questions.explanation: Moist air is forced to rise, cool and condense on the windward slope. After losing moisture, descending air on the leeward side warms and its relative humidity decreases, reducing rainfall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a rain shadow?

options.A: A relatively dry region on the leeward side of a mountain range, where descending air is warmer and drier after much of its moisture has been lost on the windward side
options.B: A region of heavy rainfall on the windward side

questions.explanation: A rain shadow is a relatively dry region on the leeward side of a mountain range, where descending air is warmer and drier after much of its moisture has been lost on the windward side.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the broad rainfall pattern in India?

options.A: Rainfall is strongly seasonal and spatially uneven; the southwest monsoon supplies most annual rainfall to much of India; very high totals occur in parts of the Western Ghats and northeast, while western Rajasthan and some rain-shadow interiors are much drier; Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share during the northeast monsoon
options.B: Rainfall is evenly distributed throughout the year
options.C: Rainfall is highest in western Rajasthan
options.D: Tamil Nadu receives most rainfall during the southwest monsoon

questions.explanation: Rainfall is strongly seasonal and spatially uneven. The southwest monsoon supplies most annual rainfall to much of India; very high totals occur in parts of the Western Ghats and northeast, while western Rajasthan and some rain-shadow interiors are much drier. Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share during the northeast monsoon.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between rainfall amount and rainfall intensity?

options.A: Amount is the total depth accumulated over a period; intensity is the rate of rainfall, often expressed in mm per hour
options.B: Amount is the rate of rainfall; intensity is the total depth
options.D: Amount is measured in mm/h; intensity is measured in mm

questions.explanation: Amount is the total depth accumulated over a period; intensity is the rate of rainfall, often expressed in mm per hour.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is weather?

options.A: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, described by temperature, humidity, cloud, wind, pressure and precipitation
options.B: The long-term statistical description of weather conditions

questions.explanation: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, described by temperature, humidity, cloud, wind, pressure and precipitation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is climate?

options.A: The short-term state of the atmosphere
options.B: The long-term statistical description of weather conditions and variability in a region, commonly assessed over a 30-year standard normal period
options.C: The daily temperature at a place
options.D: The wind speed at a place

questions.explanation: Climate is the long-term statistical description of weather conditions and variability in a region, commonly assessed over a 30-year standard normal period, although other periods may be used.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does weather differ from climate?

options.A: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term averages, ranges, variability and probabilities of weather
options.B: Weather describes long-term conditions; climate describes short-term conditions
options.D: Weather is measured in years; climate in days

questions.explanation: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term averages, ranges, variability and probabilities of weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main elements of climate?

options.A: Temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity, cloud cover, sunshine and visibility
options.B: Only temperature and rainfall

questions.explanation: The main elements of climate are temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity, cloud cover, sunshine and visibility.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major controls of climate?

options.A: Latitude; altitude; distance from sea and continentality; ocean currents; prevailing winds and air masses; pressure belts and global circulation; relief and aspect; vegetation and land cover; and human influences
options.B: Only latitude and altitude

questions.explanation: The major controls of climate include latitude; altitude; distance from sea and continentality; ocean currents; prevailing winds and air masses; pressure belts and global circulation; relief and aspect; vegetation and land cover; and human influences.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a climatic classification?

options.A: A systematic grouping of world climates based on measurable characteristics such as temperature, precipitation, seasonality and vegetation
options.B: A list of weather events
options.D: A description of a single climate

questions.explanation: A climatic classification is a systematic grouping of world climates based on measurable characteristics such as temperature, precipitation, seasonality and vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Koppen climate classification?

options.A: A widely used empirical climate classification developed by Wladimir Koppen, relating temperature and precipitation patterns to natural vegetation
options.B: A classification based only on latitude
options.C: A classification based only on ocean currents

questions.explanation: The Koppen climate classification is a widely used empirical climate classification developed by Wladimir Koppen, relating temperature and precipitation patterns to natural vegetation. Major groups are A tropical, B dry, C temperate, D continental/snow and E polar; highland climates are often treated separately or as a modifier.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group A represent?

options.A: Dry climates
options.B: Tropical climates where all months are warm; coldest-month mean generally ≥18°C

questions.explanation: Koppen group A represents tropical climates: all months warm; coldest-month mean generally ≥18°C. Subtypes include Af rainforest, Am monsoon and Aw/As savanna.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group B represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates where potential evaporation/evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation under classification criteria

questions.explanation: Koppen group B represents dry climates: potential evaporation/evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation under classification criteria. Subtypes include BW desert and BS steppe, with h hot and k cold variants.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group C represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates
options.C: Temperate climates with mild winters; coldest month below 18°C but above the D-group threshold

questions.explanation: Koppen group C represents temperate climates: mild winters; coldest month below 18°C but above the D-group threshold. Subtypes include Cf no dry season, Cw dry winter, Cs dry summer and a/b/c summer subtypes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group D represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates
options.D: Continental/snow climates with cold winters; coldest-month mean at or below about -3°C in the original/common threshold schemes; warmest month above 10°C

questions.explanation: Koppen group D represents continental/snow climates: cold winters; coldest-month mean at or below about -3°C in the original/common threshold schemes; warmest month above 10°C. Subtypes include Df, Dw, Ds and warm/cool summer subtypes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group E represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates
options.D: Polar climates where the warmest month is below 10°C; subtypes ET tundra and EF ice cap

questions.explanation: Koppen group E represents polar climates: warmest month below 10°C. Subtypes include ET tundra and EF ice cap.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group H represent?

options.A: Highland climates controlled by altitude, often used as a supplementary category with strong local variation
options.B: Hot deserts

questions.explanation: Koppen group H represents highland climates: altitude-controlled climates, often used as a supplementary category. Mountain climates with strong local variation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an equatorial climate?

options.A: A hot, humid climate near the equator with small annual temperature range, high humidity and abundant rainfall in most months, often with frequent convectional thunderstorms; Koppen Af is tropical rainforest climate
options.B: A dry climate with very low rainfall
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: An equatorial climate is a hot, humid climate near the equator with small annual temperature range, high humidity and abundant rainfall in most months, often with frequent convectional thunderstorms. Koppen Af is tropical rainforest climate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tropical monsoon climate?

options.A: A hot, humid climate with no dry season
options.B: A tropical climate with a pronounced wet season associated with monsoon circulation and a shorter dry season; Koppen Am has a short dry season but sufficient monsoon rainfall to maintain tropical vegetation
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A tropical monsoon climate is a tropical climate with a pronounced wet season associated with monsoon circulation and a shorter dry season. Koppen Am has a short dry season but sufficient monsoon rainfall to maintain tropical vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a savanna climate?

options.A: A hot, humid climate with no dry season
options.B: A tropical wet-and-dry climate with distinct rainy and dry seasons, generally supporting grassland with scattered trees; Koppen Aw or As depending on the dry season
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A savanna climate is a tropical wet-and-dry climate with distinct rainy and dry seasons, generally supporting grassland with scattered trees. Koppen Aw or As depending on the dry season.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a desert climate?

options.A: An arid climate where precipitation is very low relative to potential evapotranspiration; it may be hot (BWh) or cold (BWk); steppe climates (BS) are semi-arid
options.B: A hot, humid climate with abundant rainfall
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A desert climate is an arid climate where precipitation is very low relative to potential evapotranspiration. It may be hot (BWh) or cold (BWk); steppe climates (BS) are semi-arid.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a Mediterranean climate?

options.A: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters, commonly found on western sides of continents around 30°–45° latitude; Koppen Cs
options.B: A climate with wet summers and dry winters
options.C: A climate with rain all year and no seasonality
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A Mediterranean climate is a climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters, commonly found on western sides of continents around 30°–45° latitude. Koppen Cs.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a temperate climate?

options.A: A broad category with moderate temperatures compared with tropical and polar climates; in Koppen, C climates have mild winters and may be oceanic, humid subtropical or Mediterranean depending on precipitation and temperature seasonality
options.B: A climate with extremely cold winters
options.C: A climate with year-round high temperatures

questions.explanation: A temperate climate is a broad category with moderate temperatures compared with tropical and polar climates. In Koppen, C climates have mild winters and may be oceanic, humid subtropical or Mediterranean depending on precipitation and temperature seasonality.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a continental climate?

options.A: A climate with moderate temperatures and small annual range
options.B: A climate with large annual temperature range, commonly found in interiors and eastern parts of mid- to high-latitude continents, with cold winters and warm or hot summers; many correspond to Koppen D climates
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A continental climate is a climate with large annual temperature range, commonly found in interiors and eastern parts of mid- to high-latitude continents, with cold winters and warm or hot summers. Many correspond to Koppen D climates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tundra climate?

options.A: A polar climate in which the warmest month is above 0°C but below 10°C; vegetation is low-growing and the growing season is short; Koppen ET
options.B: A climate with permanent ice and no vegetation
options.C: A hot, humid climate near the equator
options.D: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters

questions.explanation: A tundra climate is a polar climate in which the warmest month is above 0°C but below 10°C; vegetation is low-growing and the growing season is short. Koppen ET.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an ice-cap climate?

options.A: A polar climate where the mean temperature of every month is below 0°C, preventing sustained tree or tundra vegetation; Koppen EF
options.B: A climate with warmest month above 10°C
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers
options.D: A tropical climate with abundant rainfall

questions.explanation: An ice-cap climate is a polar climate where the mean temperature of every month is below 0°C, preventing sustained tree or tundra vegetation. Koppen EF.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a highland climate?

options.A: A climate strongly controlled by elevation, slope aspect and exposure; temperature generally decreases with altitude, while precipitation varies with relief and windward/leeward position
options.B: A climate with uniform temperature throughout the year
options.D: A climate found only at sea level

questions.explanation: A highland climate is a climate strongly controlled by elevation, slope aspect and exposure. Temperature generally decreases with altitude, while precipitation varies with relief and windward/leeward position.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major climatic regions of the world?

options.A: Equatorial rainforest; tropical monsoon; tropical savanna; hot and cold deserts/steppes; Mediterranean; humid subtropical; marine west coast/oceanic; humid continental; subarctic/taiga; tundra; ice-cap; and highland regions
options.B: Only tropical and polar regions

questions.explanation: The major climatic regions of the world include equatorial rainforest; tropical monsoon; tropical savanna; hot and cold deserts/steppes; Mediterranean; humid subtropical; marine west coast/oceanic; humid continental; subarctic/taiga; tundra; ice-cap; and highland regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the limitations of the Koppen classification?

options.A: It is empirical and uses thresholds that simplify gradual transitions; it does not fully represent microclimates, wind, extreme events, soil moisture or climate change, and boundaries may differ depending on dataset and normal period
options.B: It is based entirely on wind patterns
options.D: It only applies to the Southern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: The Koppen classification is empirical and uses thresholds that simplify gradual transitions. It does not fully represent microclimates, wind, extreme events, soil moisture or climate change, and boundaries may differ depending on dataset and normal period.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does climate change affect climatic regions?

options.A: Long-term warming and shifts in precipitation can move climatic boundaries, increase heat extremes and alter drought, snow and growing-season patterns; regional changes are not uniform
options.B: Climate change has no effect on climatic regions
options.C: Climate change only affects polar regions
options.D: Climate change only affects ocean currents

questions.explanation: Long-term warming and shifts in precipitation can move climatic boundaries, increase heat extremes and alter drought, snow and growing-season patterns. Regional changes are not uniform.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a monsoon?

options.A: A seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds, accompanied by a distinct seasonal rainfall regime
options.B: A daily reversal of wind direction
options.C: A permanent wind blowing in one direction

questions.explanation: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds, accompanied by a distinct seasonal rainfall regime. The Indian monsoon is influenced by land-sea thermal contrast, seasonal migration of the ITCZ, pressure systems, topography, jet streams and ocean-atmosphere variability.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the origin of the Indian monsoon?

options.A: It results from a single factor: differential heating of land and sea
options.B: It results from interacting mechanisms: differential heating of the Asian landmass and Indian Ocean; seasonal northward shift of the ITCZ; development of low pressure over heated northwestern India and adjoining regions; cross-equatorial flow; Somali jet; Tibetan Plateau heating; and upper-air circulation changes
options.C: It is caused only by the Tibetan Plateau
options.D: It is caused only by ocean currents

questions.explanation: The Indian monsoon results from interacting mechanisms: differential heating of the Asian landmass and Indian Ocean; seasonal northward shift of the ITCZ; development of low pressure over heated northwestern India and adjoining regions; cross-equatorial flow; Somali jet; Tibetan Plateau heating; and upper-air circulation changes. No single-factor explanation is sufficient.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the southwest monsoon?

options.A: The principal summer monsoon over India, generally arriving from the southwest from June and retreating progressively from September/October onward; it has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches and supplies most annual rainfall to much of the country
options.B: The winter monsoon from the northeast
options.C: A local wind in southern India

questions.explanation: The southwest monsoon is the principal summer monsoon over India, generally arriving from the southwest from June and retreating progressively from September/October onward. It has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches and supplies most annual rainfall to much of the country.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the northeast or retreating monsoon?

options.A: The seasonal flow from the northeast during the post-monsoon period, broadly October–December; it is generally dry for much of India but picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and brings important rainfall to Tamil Nadu and parts of the southeast coast
options.B: The principal summer monsoon over India
options.C: A local wind in northern India

questions.explanation: The northeast or retreating monsoon is the seasonal flow from the northeast during the post-monsoon period, broadly October–December. It is generally dry for much of India but picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and brings important rainfall to Tamil Nadu and parts of the southeast coast.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the two main branches of the southwest monsoon?

options.A: The Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch
options.B: The Somali branch and the Tibetan branch
options.C: The Western Ghats branch and the Himalayan branch
options.D: The northeast branch and the southeast branch

questions.explanation: The two main branches of the southwest monsoon are the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch. They interact with the Western Ghats, northeast India, the Himalaya and the monsoon trough.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Arabian Sea branch affect India?

options.A: It strikes the west coast and Western Ghats, producing heavy orographic rainfall on windward slopes; it also advances into central and northwestern India and contributes to rainfall over the peninsula
options.B: It moves towards northeast India and the Ganga plains
options.C: It brings rainfall only to Tamil Nadu
options.D: It has no effect on Indian rainfall

questions.explanation: The Arabian Sea branch strikes the west coast and Western Ghats, producing heavy orographic rainfall on windward slopes. It also advances into central and northwestern India and contributes to rainfall over the peninsula.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Bay of Bengal branch affect India?

options.A: It strikes the west coast and Western Ghats
options.B: It moves towards northeast India and the Ganga plains, often producing heavy rainfall over the northeast and Himalayan foothills; it then interacts with the monsoon trough and moves west/northwest across northern India
options.C: It brings rainfall only to Tamil Nadu
options.D: It has no effect on Indian rainfall

questions.explanation: The Bay of Bengal branch moves towards northeast India and the Ganga plains, often producing heavy rainfall over the northeast and Himalayan foothills. It then interacts with the monsoon trough and moves west/northwest across northern India.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the onset of monsoon?

options.A: The arrival and establishment of sustained monsoon circulation and rainfall over a region; IMD declares onset over Kerala using defined large-scale circulation and rainfall criteria; onset dates vary from year to year
options.B: The withdrawal of monsoon from a region
options.C: A temporary weakening of monsoon rainfall
options.D: A sudden increase in rainfall after onset

questions.explanation: The onset of monsoon is the arrival and establishment of sustained monsoon circulation and rainfall over a region. IMD declares onset over Kerala using defined large-scale circulation and rainfall criteria; onset dates vary from year to year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the normal onset period over Kerala?

options.A: Around 1 June, but the actual date varies annually
options.B: Around 1 July

questions.explanation: The long-term normal onset date used by IMD is around 1 June, but the actual date varies annually. It should not be treated as a fixed date.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the withdrawal of monsoon?

options.A: The arrival and establishment of sustained monsoon circulation
options.B: The progressive retreat of southwest monsoon circulation and rainfall, beginning generally from northwest India in September and spreading towards other regions; withdrawal dates vary by year
options.C: A temporary weakening of monsoon rainfall
options.D: A sudden increase in rainfall after onset

questions.explanation: The withdrawal of monsoon is the progressive retreat of southwest monsoon circulation and rainfall, beginning generally from northwest India in September and spreading towards other regions. Withdrawal dates vary by year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the burst of monsoon?

options.A: A sudden increase in rainfall and the establishment of vigorous monsoon conditions after onset, often accompanied by widespread heavy rain; it is a descriptive term rather than a separate global circulation system
options.B: A temporary weakening of monsoon rainfall
options.C: The withdrawal of monsoon from a region
options.D: The normal onset date over Kerala

questions.explanation: The burst of monsoon is a sudden increase in rainfall and the establishment of vigorous monsoon conditions after onset, often accompanied by widespread heavy rain. It is a descriptive term rather than a separate global circulation system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a break in monsoon?

options.A: A sudden increase in rainfall after onset
options.B: A temporary weakening or shift in monsoon rainfall over much of central India, often associated with a northward displacement of the monsoon trough towards the Himalayan foothills; rain may continue or intensify in Himalayan foothill and northeast regions
options.C: The withdrawal of monsoon from a region
options.D: The normal onset date over Kerala

questions.explanation: A break in monsoon is a temporary weakening or shift in monsoon rainfall over much of central India, often associated with a northward displacement of the monsoon trough towards the Himalayan foothills. Rain may continue or intensify in Himalayan foothill and northeast regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the monsoon trough?

options.A: An elongated low-pressure zone extending across northern India during the southwest monsoon, often linking heat low regions in the west with low-pressure systems over the Bay of Bengal; its position influences rainfall distribution
options.B: A high-pressure zone over the Indian Ocean
options.D: A wind pattern in southern India

questions.explanation: The monsoon trough is an elongated low-pressure zone extending across northern India during the southwest monsoon, often linking heat low regions in the west with low-pressure systems over the Bay of Bengal. Its position influences rainfall distribution.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are western disturbances?

options.A: Eastward-moving extratropical weather systems originating or developing over the Mediterranean-West Asian region and travelling towards South Asia; they bring winter rain to northwest India and snowfall in the western Himalaya, and can interact with monsoon systems
options.B: Local winds in western India
options.C: Tropical cyclones in the Arabian Sea

questions.explanation: Western disturbances are eastward-moving extratropical weather systems originating or developing over the Mediterranean-West Asian region and travelling towards South Asia. They bring winter rain to northwest India and snowfall in the western Himalaya, and can interact with monsoon systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is El Nino?

options.A: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific associated with weakening of the normal Walker circulation; it can alter global rainfall and temperature patterns and is often associated with a weaker Indian summer monsoon, but the relationship is not deterministic
options.B: A periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific
options.C: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: El Nino is a periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific associated with weakening of the normal Walker circulation. It can alter global rainfall and temperature patterns and is often associated with a weaker Indian summer monsoon, but the relationship is not deterministic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is La Nina?

options.A: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific
options.B: A periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, generally associated with stronger-than-normal trade winds and Walker circulation; it often favours a stronger Indian monsoon, but other factors can modify the outcome
options.C: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: La Nina is a periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, generally associated with stronger-than-normal trade winds and Walker circulation. It often favours a stronger Indian monsoon, but other factors can modify the outcome.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Southern Oscillation?

options.A: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific, commonly monitored using pressure differences such as the Tahiti-Darwin index; it is the atmospheric component of ENSO
options.B: A periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific
options.C: A periodic cooling of the equatorial Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Southern Oscillation is a seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific, commonly monitored using pressure differences such as the Tahiti-Darwin index. It is the atmospheric component of ENSO.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is ENSO?

options.A: The El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon involving sea-surface temperature changes in the equatorial Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation
options.B: A type of monsoon wind
options.C: A local wind in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: ENSO is the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon involving sea-surface temperature changes in the equatorial Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)?

options.A: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern involving differences in sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean; a positive IOD often supports Indian monsoon rainfall, but its influence varies and interacts with ENSO
options.B: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and eastern Pacific
options.C: A periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific
options.D: A local wind in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is a coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern involving differences in sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean. A positive IOD often supports Indian monsoon rainfall, but its influence varies and interacts with ENSO.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO)?

options.A: A large-scale eastward-moving pulse of enhanced and suppressed tropical convection and circulation, typically recurring on intraseasonal timescales of roughly 30–60 days; its phase can modulate monsoon active and break spells
options.B: A periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific
options.C: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and eastern Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is a large-scale eastward-moving pulse of enhanced and suppressed tropical convection and circulation, typically recurring on intraseasonal timescales of roughly 30–60 days. Its phase can modulate monsoon active and break spells.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the monsoon affect Indian agriculture?

options.A: It supplies water for rain-fed crops, reservoirs and groundwater recharge; delayed onset, long breaks, uneven distribution or excess rainfall affect sowing, crop growth, yields, irrigation demand and rural livelihoods
options.B: It has no effect on agriculture

questions.explanation: The monsoon supplies water for rain-fed crops, reservoirs and groundwater recharge. Delayed onset, long breaks, uneven distribution or excess rainfall affect sowing, crop growth, yields, irrigation demand and rural livelihoods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is monsoon variability?

options.A: Variability in onset, withdrawal, total rainfall, spatial distribution, intensity and active/break spells across years and within a season; it is influenced by ENSO, IOD, MJO, land-atmosphere feedbacks, circulation and regional factors
options.B: The permanent constancy of monsoon rainfall
options.C: The daily change in monsoon winds
options.D: The seasonal reversal of winds only

questions.explanation: Monsoon variability is variability in onset, withdrawal, total rainfall, spatial distribution, intensity and active/break spells across years and within a season. It is influenced by ENSO, IOD, MJO, land-atmosphere feedbacks, circulation and regional factors.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are drought conditions?

options.A: A prolonged period of deficient precipitation or water availability relative to normal, causing meteorological, agricultural, hydrological or socioeconomic impacts; drought definitions depend on the type and region
options.B: A situation where water overflows normally dry land

questions.explanation: Drought conditions are a prolonged period of deficient precipitation or water availability relative to normal, causing meteorological, agricultural, hydrological or socioeconomic impacts. Drought definitions depend on the type and region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are flood conditions?

options.A: A prolonged period of deficient precipitation
options.B: A situation where water overflows normally dry land or river channels exceed their capacity; floods can result from intense rainfall, prolonged monsoon rain, cyclones, storm surge, snowmelt, dam releases or poor drainage

questions.explanation: Flood conditions are a situation where water overflows normally dry land or river channels exceed their capacity. Floods can result from intense rainfall, prolonged monsoon rain, cyclones, storm surge, snowmelt, dam releases or poor drainage.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why can a strong monsoon still produce drought in some areas and floods in others?

options.A: Because seasonal total rainfall can be unevenly distributed; persistent breaks, localised cloudbursts, terrain, drainage, soil moisture and reservoir operations can create contrasting impacts over short distances
options.B: Because strong monsoons always produce uniform rainfall
options.C: Because drought and floods cannot occur in the same season
options.D: Because monsoon rainfall is always predictable

questions.explanation: Seasonal total rainfall can be unevenly distributed. Persistent breaks, localised cloudbursts, terrain, drainage, soil moisture and reservoir operations can create contrasting impacts over short distances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Western Ghats influence monsoon rainfall?

options.A: The Ghats force moist Arabian Sea air to rise, causing heavy windward rainfall; the leeward Deccan interior receives less orographic rainfall and includes rain-shadow areas
options.B: The Ghats have no effect on monsoon rainfall
options.C: The Ghats cause the leeward side to receive heavy rainfall
options.D: The Ghats block all monsoon rainfall

questions.explanation: The Ghats force moist Arabian Sea air to rise, causing heavy windward rainfall. The leeward Deccan interior receives less orographic rainfall and includes rain-shadow areas.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of the Tibetan Plateau in the monsoon system?

options.A: Its elevated land surface influences upper-air heating and circulation during the warm season and is one component of the broader Asian monsoon system
options.B: It has no role in the monsoon system
options.C: It blocks monsoon winds from reaching India
options.D: It causes the monsoon to occur in winter

questions.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau's elevated land surface influences upper-air heating and circulation during the warm season and is one component of the broader Asian monsoon system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a cyclone?

options.A: A large-scale low-pressure system with winds spiralling inward near the surface; in the Northern Hemisphere the circulation is generally anticlockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere it is generally clockwise, due to the Coriolis effect
options.B: A large-scale high-pressure system

questions.explanation: A cyclone is a large-scale low-pressure system with winds spiralling inward near the surface. In the Northern Hemisphere the circulation is generally anticlockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere it is generally clockwise, due to the Coriolis effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main types of cyclones?

options.A: Tropical cyclones, extratropical or temperate cyclones, and smaller-scale phenomena such as tornadoes; their energy sources and structures differ
options.B: Only tropical cyclones

questions.explanation: The main types of cyclones are tropical cyclones, extratropical or temperate cyclones, and smaller-scale phenomena such as tornadoes. Their energy sources and structures differ.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tropical cyclone?

options.A: A cold-core, frontal, organised low-pressure system
options.B: A warm-core, non-frontal, organised low-pressure system developing over sufficiently warm tropical or subtropical oceans, with deep convection and a closed low-level circulation
options.C: A high-pressure system with sinking air
options.D: A local wind caused by terrain

questions.explanation: A tropical cyclone is a warm-core, non-frontal, organised low-pressure system developing over sufficiently warm tropical or subtropical oceans, with deep convection and a closed low-level circulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What conditions favour tropical cyclone formation?

options.A: Cold ocean water and high vertical wind shear
options.B: Warm ocean water generally at least about 26.5°C over a sufficient depth; abundant moisture; atmospheric instability; low vertical wind shear; a pre-existing disturbance and low-level convergence; and sufficient Coriolis force, so formation is uncommon very near the equator
options.D: Strong vertical wind shear and cold ocean water

questions.explanation: Conditions favouring tropical cyclone formation include warm ocean water, generally at least about 26.5°C over a sufficient depth; abundant moisture; atmospheric instability; low vertical wind shear; a pre-existing disturbance and low-level convergence; and sufficient Coriolis force, so formation is uncommon very near the equator.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does a tropical cyclone form?

options.A: A pre-existing tropical disturbance gathers warm, moist air; condensation releases latent heat, warming the core and lowering pressure; surface air converges and rises; the Coriolis force organises rotation; if environmental conditions remain favourable, the system can intensify
options.B: Cold air sinks and forms a low-pressure system
options.C: A front forms between two air masses
options.D: A high-pressure system develops over land

questions.explanation: A pre-existing tropical disturbance gathers warm, moist air. Condensation releases latent heat, warming the core and lowering pressure. Surface air converges and rises; the Coriolis force organises rotation. If environmental conditions remain favourable, the system can intensify.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the structure of a mature tropical cyclone?

options.A: A central eye (in intense systems), surrounding eyewall with strongest winds and intense rainfall, and spiral rainbands extending outward; it has a warm core and a deep circulation
options.B: A uniform layer of clouds with no distinct features
options.C: A cold core with frontal boundaries
options.D: A high-pressure centre with sinking air

questions.explanation: A mature tropical cyclone has a central eye (in intense systems), surrounding eyewall with strongest winds and intense rainfall, and spiral rainbands extending outward. It has a warm core and a deep circulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the eye of a cyclone?

options.A: The relatively calm central region of a mature tropical cyclone, often with subsiding air, light winds and sometimes clearer skies; surrounded by the eyewall
options.B: The ring of strongest winds

questions.explanation: The eye of a cyclone is the relatively calm central region of a mature tropical cyclone, often with subsiding air, light winds and sometimes clearer skies. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the eyewall of a cyclone?

options.A: The relatively calm central region with light winds
options.B: A ring of deep thunderstorms around the eye, containing the strongest sustained winds and often the heaviest rainfall
options.C: Curved bands of thunderstorms spiralling towards the centre
options.D: The outer clear zone of the cyclone

questions.explanation: The eyewall is a ring of deep thunderstorms around the eye, containing the strongest sustained winds and often the heaviest rainfall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are rainbands in a tropical cyclone?

options.A: The calm central region of the cyclone
options.B: The ring of strongest winds around the eye
options.C: Curved bands of thunderstorms spiralling towards the centre of a tropical cyclone, producing heavy rain, gusty winds and sometimes tornadoes
options.D: The outer clear zone with no weather

questions.explanation: Rainbands are curved bands of thunderstorms spiralling towards the centre of a tropical cyclone, producing heavy rain, gusty winds and sometimes tornadoes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a storm surge?

options.A: An abnormal rise of sea level above the predicted astronomical tide, driven mainly by cyclone winds pushing water towards the coast and by low atmospheric pressure
options.B: A sudden increase in wind speed during a storm
options.C: Heavy rainfall associated with a cyclone

questions.explanation: A storm surge is an abnormal rise of sea level above the predicted astronomical tide, driven mainly by cyclone winds pushing water towards the coast and by low atmospheric pressure. It can cause severe coastal inundation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is storm surge dangerous?

options.A: It can rapidly flood low-lying coasts, damage buildings and infrastructure, contaminate freshwater and cause drowning; its impact depends on storm intensity, size, track, coastal shape, bathymetry and tide timing
options.B: It only affects ships at sea
options.C: It has no impact on coastal areas

questions.explanation: Storm surge can rapidly flood low-lying coasts, damage buildings and infrastructure, contaminate freshwater and cause drowning. Its impact depends on storm intensity, size, track, coastal shape, bathymetry and tide timing.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are tropical cyclone intensities classified in the North Indian Ocean?

options.A: The India Meteorological Department uses maximum sustained wind speed categories: depression, deep depression, cyclonic storm, severe cyclonic storm, very severe cyclonic storm, extremely severe cyclonic storm and super cyclonic storm; the commonly used IMD thresholds are based on 3-minute sustained winds
options.B: They are classified only by rainfall amount
options.C: They are classified only by storm surge height
options.D: They are classified by the size of the eye

questions.explanation: The India Meteorological Department uses maximum sustained wind speed categories: depression, deep depression, cyclonic storm, severe cyclonic storm, very severe cyclonic storm, extremely severe cyclonic storm and super cyclonic storm. The commonly used IMD thresholds are based on 3-minute sustained winds.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the IMD wind speed range for a 'Cyclonic Storm'?
questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Cyclonic Storm' corresponds to 3-minute sustained wind speeds of 62–88 km/h.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the IMD wind speed range for a 'Severe Cyclonic Storm'?
questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Severe Cyclonic Storm' corresponds to 3-minute sustained wind speeds of 89–117 km/h.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the IMD wind speed range for a 'Very Severe Cyclonic Storm'?
questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Very Severe Cyclonic Storm' corresponds to 3-minute sustained wind speeds of 118–166 km/h.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the IMD wind speed range for an 'Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm'?
questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm' corresponds to 3-minute sustained wind speeds of 167–221 km/h.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: At what wind speed does the IMD category 'Super Cyclonic Storm' begin?

options.A: 62 km/h
options.B: 89 km/h

questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Super Cyclonic Storm' begins at ≥222 km/h using 3-minute sustained winds.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the IMD wind speed range for a 'Depression'?
questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Depression' corresponds to 3-minute sustained wind speeds of 31–49 km/h.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the IMD wind speed range for a 'Deep Depression'?
questions.explanation: The IMD category 'Deep Depression' corresponds to 3-minute sustained wind speeds of 50–61 km/h.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are temperate or extratropical cyclones?

options.A: Low-pressure systems of middle and high latitudes, commonly associated with fronts and strong horizontal temperature contrasts; they derive energy from baroclinic instability and often have warm and cold fronts
options.B: Warm-core, non-frontal systems over warm oceans

questions.explanation: Temperate or extratropical cyclones are low-pressure systems of middle and high latitudes, commonly associated with fronts and strong horizontal temperature contrasts. They derive energy from baroclinic instability and often have warm and cold fronts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the life cycle of a typical temperate cyclone?

options.A: A frontal wave develops along a boundary between warm and cold air; a low-pressure centre deepens; warm and cold fronts develop; the faster cold front may catch the warm front to form an occlusion; the system eventually weakens as temperature contrasts diminish
options.B: A warm ocean surface heats the air, causing it to rise and form a cyclone
options.C: A high-pressure system suddenly turns into a low-pressure system
options.D: A tornado develops into a cyclone

questions.explanation: In the life cycle of a typical temperate cyclone, a frontal wave develops along a boundary between warm and cold air; a low-pressure centre deepens; warm and cold fronts develop; the faster cold front may catch the warm front to form an occlusion; the system eventually weakens as temperature contrasts diminish.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an occluded cyclone?

options.A: A tropical cyclone with no fronts
options.B: A mature extratropical cyclone in which the cold front has overtaken the warm front, lifting the warm sector from the surface and producing an occluded front
options.C: A high-pressure system with sinking air
options.D: A cyclone that has not yet formed

questions.explanation: An occluded cyclone is a mature extratropical cyclone in which the cold front has overtaken the warm front, lifting the warm sector from the surface and producing an occluded front.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between tropical and temperate cyclones?

options.A: Tropical cyclones are warm-core, non-frontal systems powered mainly by latent heat from deep convection over warm oceans; temperate cyclones are generally cold-core or asymmetric frontal systems powered by horizontal temperature contrasts and upper-air dynamics
options.B: Tropical cyclones are cold-core and frontal; temperate cyclones are warm-core and non-frontal

questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones are warm-core, non-frontal systems powered mainly by latent heat from deep convection over warm oceans. Temperate cyclones are generally cold-core or asymmetric frontal systems powered by horizontal temperature contrasts and upper-air dynamics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a key difference between tropical and temperate cyclones?

options.A: Tropical cyclones have fronts; temperate cyclones have no fronts
options.B: Tropical cyclones are warm-core and non-frontal; temperate cyclones are usually cold-core and frontal
options.C: Tropical cyclones occur only in winter; temperate cyclones occur only in summer
options.D: Tropical cyclones are larger than temperate cyclones

questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones are warm-core and non-frontal; temperate cyclones are usually cold-core and frontal.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an anticyclone?

options.A: A low-pressure system with surface convergence and rising air
options.B: A high-pressure system with generally sinking air and outward flow near the surface; winds circulate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere; anticyclones often bring stable, settled weather, but can also cause heatwaves, cold spells or fog
options.C: A small-scale rotating column of air

questions.explanation: An anticyclone is a high-pressure system with generally sinking air and outward flow near the surface. Winds circulate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Anticyclones often bring stable, settled weather, but can also cause heatwaves, cold spells or fog.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does an anticyclone differ from a cyclone?

options.A: A cyclone is a low-pressure system with surface convergence and rising air; an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with surface divergence and generally sinking air
options.B: A cyclone is a high-pressure system; an anticyclone is a low-pressure system

questions.explanation: A cyclone is a low-pressure system with surface convergence and rising air; an anticyclone is a high-pressure system with surface divergence and generally sinking air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tornado?

options.A: A violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground; tornadoes are much smaller in scale than tropical cyclones but can produce extremely intense local winds
options.B: A large-scale low-pressure system over the ocean
options.C: A high-pressure system with sinking air

questions.explanation: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground. Tornadoes are much smaller in scale than tropical cyclones but can produce extremely intense local winds.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between a tornado and a tropical cyclone?

options.A: A tornado is a small, intense rotating column associated with severe thunderstorms; a tropical cyclone is a vast organised oceanic low-pressure system extending hundreds of kilometres
options.B: A tornado is larger than a tropical cyclone
options.C: A tornado forms over the ocean; a tropical cyclone forms over land

questions.explanation: A tornado is a small, intense rotating column associated with severe thunderstorms; a tropical cyclone is a vast organised oceanic low-pressure system extending hundreds of kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones?

options.A: Different phenomena with different causes
options.B: Regional names for the same broad phenomenon—tropical cyclones; 'hurricane' is used in the Atlantic and northeast Pacific; 'typhoon' in the northwest Pacific; 'cyclone' is used in the North Indian Ocean and South Pacific/Indian Ocean regions
options.C: Names for anticyclones in different regions
options.D: Names for tornadoes in different regions

questions.explanation: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are regional names for the same broad phenomenon—tropical cyclones. 'Hurricane' is used in the Atlantic and northeast Pacific; 'typhoon' in the northwest Pacific; 'cyclone' is used in the North Indian Ocean and South Pacific/Indian Ocean regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tropical storm?

options.A: A named tropical cyclone that has reached a basin-specific sustained-wind threshold; the wind averaging period and naming threshold differ among meteorological agencies, so category labels should not be compared without checking the standard used
options.B: A storm that forms over land

questions.explanation: A tropical storm is a named tropical cyclone that has reached a basin-specific sustained-wind threshold. The wind averaging period and naming threshold differ among meteorological agencies, so category labels should not be compared without checking the standard used.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which regions of India are cyclone-prone?

options.A: The east coast bordering the Bay of Bengal is particularly exposed, including Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal; Gujarat and Maharashtra on the Arabian Sea coast are also exposed; islands and other coastal areas face risks
options.B: Only the west coast is cyclone-prone
options.C: Only the interior regions are cyclone-prone
options.D: No region of India is cyclone-prone

questions.explanation: The east coast bordering the Bay of Bengal is particularly exposed, including Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. Gujarat and Maharashtra on the Arabian Sea coast are also exposed; islands and other coastal areas face risks.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why has the Bay of Bengal historically experienced many severe cyclone impacts?

options.A: It is a warm, semi-enclosed basin with favourable cyclone environments, and its northern shape, shallow coastal waters, low-lying deltaic coast and dense population can amplify storm-surge impacts
options.B: It is a cold, deep ocean with no cyclone formation
options.D: It is located at the equator where Coriolis force is zero

questions.explanation: The Bay of Bengal is a warm, semi-enclosed basin with favourable cyclone environments, and its northern shape, shallow coastal waters, low-lying deltaic coast and dense population can amplify storm-surge impacts. Arabian Sea cyclones also occur and can be severe.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Do Arabian Sea cyclones occur?

options.A: No, the Arabian Sea never experiences cyclones
options.B: Yes, the Arabian Sea produces tropical cyclones, including severe systems; their frequency and intensity vary, and recent decades have shown important changes
options.D: Yes, but they are always weak

questions.explanation: Yes, the Arabian Sea produces tropical cyclones, including severe systems. Their frequency and intensity vary, and recent decades have shown important changes; do not assume the Arabian Sea is cyclone-free.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the cyclone warning system in India?

options.B: There is no cyclone warning system in India
options.C: Cyclone warnings are issued only by international agencies
options.D: Cyclone warnings are based only on satellite images

questions.explanation: The India Meteorological Department monitors weather using satellites, radar, ocean observations and numerical models, issues forecasts and staged warnings, and disseminates alerts to disaster-management agencies, ports, fisheries and the public. INCOIS provides ocean-state and storm-surge-related services and advisories.

questions.question: What safety actions are important before and during a cyclone?

questions.explanation: The troposphere is characterised by temperature generally decreasing with altitude and contains most water vapour and weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which atmospheric layer is characterised by temperature increasing with altitude due to ozone absorption?

options.A: Troposphere
options.B: Stratosphere

questions.explanation: The stratosphere is characterised by temperature increasing with height through much of it because ozone absorbs ultraviolet solar radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which atmospheric layer is characterised by temperature decreasing with altitude and where many meteors burn up?

options.A: Troposphere
options.B: Stratosphere

questions.explanation: The mesosphere is characterised by temperature decreasing with altitude and many incoming meteoroids ablate in this region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which atmospheric layer is characterised by temperature rising sharply with height due to absorption of high-energy solar radiation?

options.A: Troposphere
options.B: Stratosphere

questions.explanation: In the thermosphere, temperature rises markedly with height because sparse gas molecules absorb high-energy solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the exosphere?

options.A: The lowest atmospheric layer with most weather
options.B: The layer where ozone absorbs UV radiation
options.C: The outermost atmospheric region where gas particles are so far apart that collisions are infrequent and it gradually merges with interplanetary space
options.D: The layer where meteors burn up

questions.explanation: The exosphere is the outermost atmospheric region, where gas particles are so far apart that collisions are infrequent. It gradually merges with interplanetary space.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the primary cause of ozone depletion?

options.A: Carbon dioxide emissions
options.B: Chlorine- and bromine-containing compounds from CFCs and halons

questions.explanation: Chlorine- and bromine-containing compounds, notably from older chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons, release reactive halogens in the stratosphere that catalytically destroy ozone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which international agreement has been instrumental in phasing down ozone-depleting substances?

options.A: Kyoto Protocol
options.B: Paris Agreement

questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol has phased down many ozone-depleting substances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the greenhouse effect?

options.A: The cooling of Earth's surface due to reflection of sunlight
options.B: The natural warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation
options.C: The transfer of heat by conduction from the ground
options.D: The depletion of the ozone layer

questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the natural warming of Earth's surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which gas is the largest natural contributor to the greenhouse effect?

options.A: Carbon dioxide
options.B: Methane

questions.explanation: Water vapour is the largest natural contributor to the greenhouse effect but mainly acts as a feedback; CO2 and other long-lived gases are major drivers of current human-caused warming.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between global warming and climate change?

options.A: They are exactly the same thing
options.B: Global warming refers specifically to the rise in global mean temperature; climate change includes wider long-term changes such as rainfall patterns, extremes, sea level, snow and ice, and ocean conditions
options.C: Climate change refers only to temperature rise
options.D: Global warming refers only to sea-level rise

questions.explanation: Global warming refers specifically to the rise in global mean temperature. Climate change includes wider long-term changes such as rainfall patterns, extremes, sea level, snow and ice, and ocean conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the normal environmental lapse rate?

options.A: The rate at which an unsaturated rising air parcel cools, about 9.8°C per kilometre
options.B: The average rate at which environmental air temperature decreases with altitude in the troposphere, approximately 6.5°C per kilometre globally
options.C: The rate at which temperature increases with altitude
options.D: The rate of temperature change at the equator only

questions.explanation: The normal or average environmental lapse rate is the average rate at which environmental air temperature decreases with altitude in the troposphere, approximately 6.5°C per kilometre globally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the dry adiabatic lapse rate?

options.A: The average environmental lapse rate of 6.5°C per kilometre
options.B: The rate at which an unsaturated rising air parcel cools by expansion, about 9.8°C per kilometre
options.C: The rate at which temperature increases with altitude
options.D: The rate of cooling of saturated air

questions.explanation: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is the rate at which an unsaturated rising air parcel cools by expansion, about 9.8°C per kilometre.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a temperature inversion?

options.A: A condition in which temperature decreases with height
options.B: A condition in which air temperature increases with height through a layer, instead of decreasing
options.C: A condition in which pressure is constant
options.D: A condition in which wind stops everywhere

questions.explanation: Temperature inversion is a condition in which air temperature increases with height through a layer, instead of decreasing.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a common type of temperature inversion?

options.A: Radiation inversion on clear, calm nights
options.B: Valley or cold-air-pooling inversion
options.C: Subsidence inversion under sinking air in high-pressure systems

questions.explanation: Common types of temperature inversion include radiation inversion on clear, calm nights; valley or cold-air-pooling inversion; subsidence inversion under sinking air in high-pressure systems; and frontal inversion where warm air overrides colder air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the standard sea-level pressure?

options.B: 760 hPa

questions.explanation: Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hPa = 1013.25 mb = 760 mm Hg (approx.).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are isobars?

options.A: Lines joining places with equal temperature
options.B: Lines on a weather map joining places with equal atmospheric pressure at a specified time
options.C: Lines joining places with equal rainfall
options.D: Lines joining places with equal wind speed

questions.explanation: Isobars are lines on a weather map joining places with equal atmospheric pressure at a specified time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What do closely spaced isobars indicate?

options.A: A weak pressure gradient and light winds
options.B: A steep pressure gradient and usually stronger winds

questions.explanation: Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient and usually stronger winds, all else equal.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a high-pressure area or anticyclone?

options.A: A region where pressure is lower than surrounding areas
options.B: A region where pressure is higher than surrounding areas, with air generally diverging outward and sinking from aloft

questions.explanation: A high-pressure area or anticyclone is a region where pressure is higher than surrounding areas. Near the surface, air generally diverges outward and sinks from aloft.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a low-pressure area or depression?

options.A: A region where pressure is higher than surrounding areas
options.B: A region where pressure is lower than surrounding areas, with air generally converging and rising

questions.explanation: A low-pressure area or depression is a region where pressure is lower than surrounding areas. Near the surface, air generally converges and rises, favouring cloud formation and precipitation if moisture and instability are present.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What causes the equatorial low-pressure belt?

options.A: Cold descending air
options.B: Strong solar heating warms air, which rises in a broad zone near the thermal equator; convergence of trade winds in the ITCZ reinforces the low-pressure belt

questions.explanation: Strong solar heating warms air, which rises in a broad zone near the thermal equator. Convergence of trade winds in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) reinforces the low-pressure belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the subtropical high-pressure belt?

options.A: A belt of low pressure near the equator
options.B: A belt of high pressure near 25°–35° latitude in both hemispheres, associated with descending branches of the Hadley circulation
options.C: A belt of low pressure near 50°–70° latitude
options.D: A high-pressure region near the poles

questions.explanation: The subtropical high-pressure belt is a belt of high pressure near 25°–35° latitude in both hemispheres, associated with descending branches of the Hadley circulation. It is often called the horse-latitude belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is another name for the subtropical high-pressure belt?

options.A: Doldrums
options.B: Horse-latitude belt

questions.explanation: The subtropical high-pressure belt is often called the horse-latitude belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What causes the subpolar low-pressure belt?

options.A: Strong solar heating near the equator
options.B: Near 50°–70° latitude, relatively warm westerlies meet cold polar easterlies along the polar front; convergence and rising air help form a belt of low pressure, especially over oceans
options.C: Descending air from the Hadley circulation
options.D: Cold dense air near the poles

questions.explanation: Near 50°–70° latitude, relatively warm westerlies meet cold polar easterlies along the polar front. Convergence and rising air help form a belt of low pressure, especially over oceans.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the polar high-pressure belt?

options.A: A low-pressure region near the poles
options.B: A high-pressure region near the poles, associated with very cold, dense air and subsidence
options.C: A high-pressure region near the equator

questions.explanation: The polar high-pressure belt is a high-pressure region near the poles, associated with very cold, dense air and subsidence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are pressure belts not fixed at exact latitudes?

options.A: They are fixed permanently
options.B: They shift seasonally with the apparent movement of the Sun and the thermal equator, and are modified by continents, oceans, topography and seasonal heating
options.C: They only shift due to ocean currents
options.D: They only shift due to volcanic activity

questions.explanation: Pressure belts are not fixed at exact latitudes because they shift seasonally with the apparent movement of the Sun and the thermal equator, and are modified by continents, oceans, topography and seasonal heating.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the pressure gradient force?

options.A: The force caused by Earth's rotation
options.B: The force arising from differences in pressure over distance; it accelerates air from high towards low pressure
options.D: The force caused by gravity only

questions.explanation: The pressure gradient force arises from differences in pressure over distance; it accelerates air from high towards low pressure, though Earth's rotation and friction modify the resulting wind.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is wind?

options.A: The vertical movement of air only
options.B: The horizontal movement of air relative to Earth's surface, primarily driven by pressure differences
options.C: The movement of water in the ocean

questions.explanation: Wind is the horizontal movement of air relative to Earth's surface, primarily driven by pressure differences. Its direction and speed are modified by the Coriolis force, friction and local terrain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are winds classified geographically?

options.A: Only by speed
options.B: Only by direction
options.C: Planetary or permanent winds; periodic or seasonal winds; and local winds

questions.explanation: Winds are broadly classified geographically as planetary or permanent winds; periodic or seasonal winds; and local winds. Synoptic-scale winds also include cyclonic and anticyclonic circulations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are planetary winds?

options.A: Local winds caused by terrain
options.B: Large-scale prevailing winds associated with global pressure belts and atmospheric circulation: trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies

questions.explanation: Planetary winds are large-scale prevailing winds associated with global pressure belts and atmospheric circulation: trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are trade winds?

options.A: Prevailing westerly winds in middle latitudes
options.B: Persistent easterly winds blowing from subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low; they blow from northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere
options.C: Cold easterly winds from polar regions

questions.explanation: Trade winds are persistent easterly winds blowing from subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low. They blow from northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are westerlies?

options.A: Easterly winds in the tropics
options.B: Prevailing winds flowing from subtropical highs towards subpolar lows, generally from west to east in the middle latitudes
options.C: Cold easterly winds from polar regions

questions.explanation: Westerlies are prevailing winds flowing from subtropical highs towards subpolar lows, generally from west to east in the middle latitudes. They are often stronger and more variable in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are polar easterlies?

options.A: Warm, moist westerly winds in middle latitudes
options.B: Cold, generally dry easterly winds flowing outward from polar high-pressure areas towards subpolar low-pressure regions
