questions.explanation: Polar easterlies are cold, generally dry easterly winds flowing outward from polar high-pressure areas towards subpolar low-pressure regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are periodic winds?

options.A: Winds that blow constantly in one direction
options.B: Winds that reverse or change direction at regular intervals, such as monsoon winds, land and sea breezes, and mountain and valley breezes

questions.explanation: Periodic winds are winds that reverse or change direction at regular intervals, such as monsoon winds (seasonal), land and sea breezes (daily), and mountain and valley breezes (daily).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a monsoon wind?

options.A: A daily reversing wind system
options.B: A seasonally reversing wind system associated with seasonal differences in heating and pressure between land and ocean, modified by topography, large-scale circulation and ocean-atmosphere interactions
options.D: A local wind caused by terrain only

questions.explanation: A monsoon wind is a seasonally reversing wind system associated with seasonal differences in heating and pressure between land and ocean, modified by topography, large-scale circulation and ocean-atmosphere interactions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a sea breeze?

options.A: A nighttime coastal wind blowing from land to sea
options.B: A daytime coastal wind blowing from sea to land because land heats faster than the sea, creating relatively lower pressure over land

questions.explanation: A sea breeze is a daytime coastal wind blowing from sea to land because land heats faster than the sea, creating relatively lower pressure over land.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a land breeze?

options.A: A daytime coastal wind blowing from sea to land
options.B: A nighttime coastal wind blowing from land to sea because land cools faster than the sea, creating relatively higher pressure over land

questions.explanation: A land breeze is a nighttime coastal wind blowing from land to sea because land cools faster than the sea, creating relatively higher pressure over land.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a valley breeze?

options.A: A nighttime downslope flow of cooled, dense air
options.B: A daytime upslope wind caused by heating of mountain slopes and adjacent air, which rises and draws air up-valley

questions.explanation: A valley breeze is a daytime upslope wind caused by heating of mountain slopes and adjacent air, which rises and draws air up-valley.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a mountain breeze?

options.A: A daytime upslope wind
options.B: A nighttime downslope flow of cooled, dense air from mountain slopes into valleys

questions.explanation: A mountain breeze is a nighttime downslope flow of cooled, dense air from mountain slopes into valleys.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Loo?

options.A: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.B: A hot, dry summer wind over northwestern and northern India, especially the Indo-Gangetic plain
options.C: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Loo is a hot, dry summer wind over northwestern and northern India, especially the Indo-Gangetic plain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Chinook?

options.A: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.B: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains in North America that can rapidly raise temperature
options.C: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Chinook is a warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains in North America; it can rapidly raise temperature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Foehn or Föhn?

options.A: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.B: A warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of the Alps, similar to Chinook
options.C: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Foehn or Föhn is a warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of the Alps; similar to Chinook.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Mistral?

options.A: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.B: A cold, strong northerly or northwesterly wind channelled down the Rhône Valley towards the Gulf of Lion
options.C: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Mistral is a cold, strong northerly or northwesterly wind channelled down the Rhône Valley towards the Gulf of Lion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Sirocco?

options.A: A cold, gusty downslope wind along the Adriatic coast
options.B: A hot, often dusty wind originating over the Sahara and moving towards the Mediterranean; may become humid over the sea
options.C: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Sirocco is a hot, often dusty wind originating over the Sahara and moving towards the Mediterranean; it may become humid over the sea.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Harmattan?

options.A: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.B: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa, especially in boreal winter
options.C: A cold, strong northerly wind in the Rhône Valley
options.D: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains

questions.explanation: The Harmattan is a dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa, especially in boreal winter.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Bora?

options.A: A warm, dry downslope wind east of the Rocky Mountains
options.B: A cold, gusty downslope wind along the Adriatic coast, especially near the eastern Adriatic
options.C: A hot, dry summer wind over northern India
options.D: A dry, dusty northeast trade wind affecting West Africa

questions.explanation: The Bora is a cold, gusty downslope wind along the Adriatic coast, especially near the eastern Adriatic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are local winds?

options.A: Winds that blow across the entire globe
options.B: Winds affecting limited regions, often produced by local pressure and temperature contrasts or terrain
options.C: Winds that blow only at the equator
options.D: Winds that blow only at the poles

questions.explanation: Local winds are winds affecting limited regions, often produced by local pressure and temperature contrasts or terrain. Their names and effects vary geographically.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Coriolis force?

options.A: A force caused by pressure differences
options.B: An apparent deflection of moving air and water caused by Earth's rotation; it deflects motion to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
options.D: A force caused by gravity only

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is an apparent deflection of moving air and water caused by Earth's rotation. It deflects motion to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere; it is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which direction does the Coriolis force deflect moving air in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.A: To the left
options.B: To the right

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force deflects motion to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Coriolis force zero?

options.A: At the poles
options.B: At the equator

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does the Coriolis force change the speed of wind directly?

options.A: Yes, it increases wind speed
options.B: Yes, it decreases wind speed
options.C: No, it changes direction, not speed directly
options.D: Yes, it both increases and decreases speed

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force changes direction, not speed directly.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are jet streams?

options.A: Wide bands of light winds near the surface
options.B: Narrow bands of very strong winds near the tropopause, generally flowing west to east

questions.explanation: Jet streams are narrow bands of very strong winds near the tropopause, generally flowing west to east. Major types include polar-front and subtropical jet streams; their position and strength vary seasonally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major types of jet streams?

options.A: Equatorial and polar jet streams only
options.B: Polar-front and subtropical jet streams
options.C: Monsoon and trade wind jet streams
options.D: Land and sea breeze jet streams

questions.explanation: Major types include polar-front and subtropical jet streams; their position and strength vary seasonally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do jet streams influence the Indian monsoon?

options.A: Jet streams have no influence on the monsoon
options.B: Jet streams steer weather systems and influence upper-air divergence and circulation; seasonal shifts, including the northward movement of the subtropical westerly jet and establishment of the tropical easterly jet, are associated with the seasonal evolution of the Indian monsoon
options.C: Jet streams only affect winter weather
options.D: Jet streams only affect ocean currents

questions.explanation: Jet streams steer weather systems and influence upper-air divergence and circulation. Seasonal shifts, including the northward movement of the subtropical westerly jet and establishment of the tropical easterly jet, are associated with the seasonal evolution of the Indian monsoon.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are Rossby waves?

options.A: Small-scale waves in the ocean
options.B: Large-scale meanders in the westerly flow of the atmosphere, caused by the variation of the Coriolis parameter with latitude and influenced by topography and temperature contrasts
options.D: Waves in the trade winds only

questions.explanation: Rossby waves are large-scale meanders in the westerly flow of the atmosphere, caused by the variation of the Coriolis parameter with latitude and influenced by topography and temperature contrasts. They help steer weather systems and can produce persistent weather patterns.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an air mass?

options.A: A small pocket of air near the ground
options.B: A large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity over a broad horizontal area, acquired from its source region
options.D: A region of high pressure only

questions.explanation: An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity over a broad horizontal area, acquired from its source region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are air masses classified?

options.A: Only by temperature
options.B: Only by humidity
options.C: By moisture source: continental (c, relatively dry) or maritime (m, moist); and by thermal character/latitude: Arctic or Antarctic (A/AA), polar (P) and tropical (T)

questions.explanation: Air masses are classified by moisture source: continental (c, relatively dry) or maritime (m, moist); and by thermal character/latitude: Arctic or Antarctic (A/AA), polar (P) and tropical (T). Combined labels include cP, mP, cT and mT.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a front?

options.A: A type of cloud
options.B: A boundary or transition zone separating air masses with contrasting temperature and density

questions.explanation: A front is a boundary or transition zone separating air masses with contrasting temperature and density. Weather changes often occur along fronts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a warm front?

options.A: A front where advancing cold air undercuts warm air
options.B: A front where advancing warm air rises gradually over retreating cold air, commonly producing widespread layered clouds and steady precipitation ahead of the surface front
options.C: A front formed when a cold front catches up with a warm front
options.D: A boundary between two air masses of the same temperature

questions.explanation: A warm front is a front where advancing warm air rises gradually over retreating cold air. It commonly produces widespread layered clouds and steady precipitation ahead of the surface front.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a cold front?

options.A: A front where advancing warm air rises over cold air
options.B: A front where advancing cold, dense air undercuts warm air and forces it to rise more steeply, potentially producing showers, thunderstorms and a relatively abrupt temperature change
options.C: A front formed when a cold front catches up with a warm front
options.D: A boundary between two air masses of the same temperature

questions.explanation: A cold front is a front where advancing cold, dense air undercuts warm air and forces it to rise more steeply. It may produce showers, thunderstorms and a relatively abrupt temperature change.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an occluded front?

options.A: A front where advancing warm air rises over cold air
options.B: A front where advancing cold air undercuts warm air
options.C: A front formed when a faster-moving cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm air off the ground
options.D: A boundary between two air masses of the same temperature

questions.explanation: An occluded front is a front formed when a faster-moving cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm air off the ground. It is commonly associated with a mature mid-latitude cyclone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does a warm front differ from a cold front?

options.A: Warm fronts are steeper and bring intense showers
options.B: Warm fronts usually have a gentler slope and broader, steadier precipitation; cold fronts are steeper and may bring narrower bands of intense showers or thunderstorms
options.C: Cold fronts have a gentler slope and broader precipitation
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: Warm fronts usually have a gentler slope and broader, steadier precipitation; cold fronts are steeper and may bring narrower bands of intense showers or thunderstorms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is friction's role in wind?

options.A: Friction increases wind speed near the surface
options.B: Friction slows wind near the surface and reduces the Coriolis deflection, causing surface winds to cross isobars towards lower pressure; friction decreases with height
options.C: Friction has no effect on wind
options.D: Friction only affects wind at high altitudes

questions.explanation: Friction slows wind near the surface and reduces the Coriolis deflection, causing surface winds to cross isobars towards lower pressure. Friction decreases with height.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is humidity?

options.A: The amount of oxygen present in the air
options.B: The amount of water vapour present in the air

questions.explanation: Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in the air. It may be expressed as absolute humidity, specific humidity, mixing ratio or relative humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is absolute humidity?

options.A: The mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air
options.B: The mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, commonly expressed in grams per cubic metre (g/m³)
options.C: The ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, commonly expressed in grams per cubic metre (g/m³). It changes when air volume changes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is specific humidity?

options.A: The mass of water vapour per unit volume of air
options.B: The mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air, usually expressed in grams per kilogram (g/kg)
options.C: The ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Specific humidity is the mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air, usually expressed in grams per kilogram (g/kg). It is useful because it is less affected by changes in air volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is relative humidity?

options.A: The mass of water vapour per unit volume of air
options.B: The mass of water vapour per unit mass of moist air
options.C: The ratio of actual water-vapour pressure to saturation water-vapour pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes saturated

questions.explanation: Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water-vapour pressure to saturation water-vapour pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage. It depends strongly on temperature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is dew point?

options.A: The temperature at which water freezes
options.B: The temperature to which air must be cooled, at approximately constant pressure and water-vapour content, for it to become saturated
options.C: The temperature at which water boils
options.D: The temperature at which air becomes unsaturated

questions.explanation: Dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, at approximately constant pressure and water-vapour content, for it to become saturated. Dew point is a useful indicator of actual atmospheric moisture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is saturation?

options.A: A state in which air contains no water vapour
options.B: A state in which air contains the maximum water vapour possible at a given temperature and pressure, so relative humidity is approximately 100%
options.C: A state in which air is unsaturated
options.D: A state in which air is frozen

questions.explanation: Saturation is a state in which air contains the maximum water vapour possible at a given temperature and pressure, so relative humidity is approximately 100%.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is evaporation?

options.A: The change of water vapour into liquid water
options.B: The change of liquid water into water vapour from a surface; it consumes latent heat and is promoted by warmth, wind and low humidity
options.C: The change of ice into water
options.D: The change of water into ice

questions.explanation: Evaporation is the change of liquid water into water vapour from a surface. It consumes latent heat and is promoted by warmth, wind and low humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is condensation?

options.A: The change of liquid water into water vapour
options.B: The change of water vapour into liquid water when air reaches saturation and vapour condenses on suitable surfaces or particles; it releases latent heat
options.C: The change of ice into water
options.D: The change of water into ice

questions.explanation: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid water when air reaches saturation and vapour condenses on suitable surfaces or particles. It releases latent heat.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of condensation nuclei?

options.A: They absorb sunlight
options.B: Tiny particles such as sea salt, dust and aerosols provide surfaces on which water vapour can condense to form cloud droplets
options.C: They increase the temperature of the air
options.D: They decrease the humidity of the air

questions.explanation: Tiny particles such as sea salt, dust and aerosols provide surfaces on which water vapour can condense to form cloud droplets. Ice-nucleating particles help ice crystals form.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do clouds form?

options.A: Dust particles combine to form clouds
options.B: Moist air cools to its dew point, commonly through uplift and expansion, and becomes saturated; water vapour condenses onto cloud-condensation nuclei or deposits as ice crystals, forming visible droplets or crystals
options.C: Water vapour rises directly as liquid

questions.explanation: Moist air cools to its dew point, commonly through uplift and expansion, and becomes saturated. Water vapour condenses onto cloud-condensation nuclei or deposits as ice crystals, forming visible droplets or crystals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the four basic cloud-form names?

options.A: Cirrus, altus, stratus and nimbus
options.B: Cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus

questions.explanation: The four basic cloud-form names are cirrus (fibrous/high), cumulus (heap-like), stratus (layer-like) and nimbus (rain-bearing). These combining forms create many cloud genera, such as cumulonimbus and nimbostratus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are cirrus clouds?

options.A: Heap-shaped clouds with flat bases
options.B: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds; often fair at present, increasing cirrus can precede a change

questions.explanation: Cirrus (Ci) clouds are high, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds. Often fair at present; increasing cirrus can precede a change.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are cumulus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Heap-shaped clouds with flat bases; usually low to middle levels; fair-weather cumulus if small, may grow into showers

questions.explanation: Cumulus (Cu) clouds are heap-shaped clouds with flat bases, usually at low to middle levels. Fair-weather cumulus if small; may grow into showers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are stratus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Heap-shaped clouds with flat bases
options.C: Uniform low grey layers; overcast skies, drizzle or mist-like conditions

questions.explanation: Stratus (St) clouds are uniform low grey layers. They produce overcast skies, drizzle or mist-like conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does the term 'nimbus' indicate in cloud names?

options.A: High altitude
options.B: Rain-bearing

questions.explanation: Nimbus is a rain-bearing descriptor, not a standalone modern cloud genus. It is used in names such as nimbostratus and cumulonimbus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are cumulonimbus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Heap-shaped fair-weather clouds
options.D: Deep, vertically developed thunderstorm clouds associated with heavy showers, lightning, hail, gusts and sometimes severe weather

questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus (Cb) clouds are deep, vertically developed thunderstorm clouds. They are associated with heavy showers, lightning, hail, gusts and sometimes severe weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are nimbostratus clouds?

options.A: High, thin, wispy ice-crystal clouds
options.B: Thick, widespread layered clouds producing persistent, widespread rain or snow

questions.explanation: Nimbostratus (Ns) clouds are thick, widespread layered clouds. They produce persistent, widespread rain or snow.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are clouds classified by height and form?

options.A: Clouds are classified only by color
options.B: The World Meteorological Organization recognises ten principal cloud genera, commonly grouped as high clouds, middle clouds, low clouds and clouds with vertical development
options.C: Clouds are classified only by temperature
options.D: Clouds are classified only by wind speed

questions.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization recognises ten principal cloud genera, commonly grouped as high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus), middle clouds (altostratus, altocumulus), low clouds (stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus) and clouds with vertical development (cumulus and cumulonimbus). Height boundaries vary with latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as high clouds?

options.A: Altostratus and altocumulus
options.B: Cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus

questions.explanation: High clouds include cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as middle clouds?

options.A: Cirrus and cirrostratus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: Middle clouds include altostratus and altocumulus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as low clouds?

options.A: Cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: Low clouds include stratus, stratocumulus and nimbostratus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which clouds are classified as clouds with vertical development?

options.A: Cirrus and cirrostratus
options.B: Altostratus and altocumulus

questions.explanation: Clouds with vertical development include cumulus and cumulonimbus.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is fog?

options.A: A cloud high in the stratosphere
options.B: A cloud at or very near the ground that reduces horizontal visibility, conventionally to less than 1 km in meteorological reporting

questions.explanation: Fog is a cloud at or very near the ground that reduces horizontal visibility, conventionally to less than 1 km in meteorological reporting.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is mist?

options.A: A cloud at high altitude
options.B: A suspension of tiny water droplets near the ground that reduces visibility, but generally less severely than fog; a common convention is visibility of 1 km or more

questions.explanation: Mist is a suspension of tiny water droplets near the ground that reduces visibility, but generally less severely than fog; a common convention is visibility of 1 km or more.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is dew?

options.A: Ice crystals formed by deposition of water vapour
options.B: Liquid water droplets formed when a surface cools to or below the dew point and water vapour condenses on it

questions.explanation: Dew is liquid water droplets formed when a surface cools to or below the dew point and water vapour condenses on it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is frost?

options.A: Liquid water droplets formed by condensation
options.B: Ice crystals formed by deposition of water vapour or freezing of dew when it is sufficiently cold

questions.explanation: Frost is ice crystals formed by deposition of water vapour or freezing of dew when it is sufficiently cold.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is hail?

options.A: Small ice pellets formed when raindrops refreeze
options.B: Balls or irregular lumps of ice produced in strong cumulonimbus updrafts, where ice particles grow by collecting supercooled water droplets before falling
options.C: Ice crystals that form on surfaces

questions.explanation: Hail is balls or irregular lumps of ice produced in strong cumulonimbus updrafts, where ice particles grow by collecting supercooled water droplets before falling.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is hail different from sleet?

options.A: Hail is small ice pellets; sleet is large ice balls
options.B: Hail grows in strong thunderstorm updrafts and can become large; sleet is generally small ice pellets formed when raindrops or partially melted snow refreeze before reaching the ground
options.C: Hail and sleet are the same thing
options.D: Hail forms on surfaces; sleet falls from clouds

questions.explanation: Hail grows in strong thunderstorm updrafts and can become large; sleet is generally small ice pellets formed when raindrops or partially melted snow refreeze before reaching the ground. Usage of 'sleet' differs between regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is latent heat?

options.A: Heat transferred by conduction
options.B: Energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature

questions.explanation: Latent heat is energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature. Evaporation absorbs latent heat; condensation, freezing and deposition release it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does relative humidity rise when air cools without adding water vapour?

options.A: Because water vapour is added to the air
options.B: Because saturation vapour pressure decreases as temperature falls, so the same actual vapour content becomes a larger fraction of saturation

questions.explanation: Saturation vapour pressure decreases as temperature falls. The same actual vapour content therefore becomes a larger fraction of saturation, raising relative humidity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is precipitation?

options.A: Only rainfall
options.B: Any form of water, liquid or solid, falling from clouds or the atmosphere to Earth's surface, including rain, drizzle, snow, sleet and hail

questions.explanation: Precipitation is any form of water, liquid or solid, falling from clouds or the atmosphere to Earth's surface, including rain, drizzle, snow, sleet and hail. Dew and frost form on surfaces and are not precipitation in the strict meteorological sense.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are dew and frost considered precipitation in the strict meteorological sense?

options.A: Yes, they are precipitation
options.B: No, they form on surfaces and are not precipitation in the strict meteorological sense

questions.explanation: Dew and frost form on surfaces and are not precipitation in the strict meteorological sense.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is rainfall?

options.A: Solid precipitation only
options.B: Liquid precipitation consisting of water droplets that fall from clouds and reach the ground

questions.explanation: Rainfall is liquid precipitation consisting of water droplets that fall from clouds and reach the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is convectional rainfall?

options.A: Rain produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier
options.B: Rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise, expand and cool adiabatically, reach saturation and form clouds, often cumulonimbus; commonly produces intense, short-duration showers and thunderstorms
options.C: Precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise, expand and cool adiabatically, reach saturation and form clouds, often cumulonimbus. It commonly produces intense, short-duration showers and thunderstorms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is convectional rainfall common?

options.A: Polar regions only
options.B: Equatorial regions, tropical interiors and warm-season continental areas where surface heating and moisture are strong

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is common in equatorial regions, tropical interiors and warm-season continental areas where surface heating and moisture are strong.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is orographic rainfall?

options.A: Rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise
options.B: Rainfall produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier; it cools, condenses and precipitates on the windward slope, creating a rain-shadow effect on the leeward side
options.C: Precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts

questions.explanation: Orographic rainfall is rainfall produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier. It cools, condenses and precipitates on the windward slope; descending air on the leeward side becomes warmer and drier, creating a rain-shadow effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is another name for orographic rainfall?

options.A: Convectional rainfall
options.B: Cyclonic rainfall

questions.explanation: Relief rainfall is another name for orographic rainfall, emphasising the role of topography or relief in forcing air upward.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is cyclonic or frontal rainfall?

options.A: Rain produced when strong surface heating causes moist air to rise
options.B: Rainfall produced when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier
options.C: Precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts, where converging air rises; occurs in tropical cyclones and in temperate depressions along warm, cold and occluded fronts

questions.explanation: Cyclonic or frontal rainfall is precipitation associated with low-pressure systems and fronts, where converging air rises. It occurs in tropical cyclones and in temperate depressions along warm, cold and occluded fronts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of rainfall is characterised by intense, localised showers and often thunderstorm activity?

options.A: Orographic rainfall
options.B: Cyclonic rainfall

questions.explanation: Convectional rainfall is characterised by intense, localised showers and often thunderstorm activity due to surface heating and buoyant rising air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of rainfall produces windward rain and a leeward rain shadow?

options.A: Convectional rainfall
options.B: Orographic or relief rainfall

questions.explanation: Orographic or relief rainfall produces windward rain and a leeward rain shadow.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which type of rainfall is typically widespread and often longer-lasting?

options.A: Convectional rainfall
options.B: Orographic rainfall

questions.explanation: Cyclonic or frontal rainfall is typically widespread and often longer-lasting due to convergence and frontal overrunning.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is snowfall?

options.A: Rain that freezes after hitting the ground
options.B: Precipitation in the form of ice crystals or snowflakes that reach the ground without melting completely; requires a sufficiently cold atmospheric column and surface conditions
options.C: Ice pellets formed when raindrops refreeze

questions.explanation: Snowfall is precipitation in the form of ice crystals or snowflakes that reach the ground without melting completely. It requires a sufficiently cold atmospheric column and surface conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is sleet?

options.A: Large ice balls produced in thunderstorm updrafts
options.B: A term with regional differences; in many meteorological contexts it refers to small ice pellets formed when melted or partially melted snow refreezes in a subfreezing layer near the ground

questions.explanation: Sleet is a term with regional differences. In many meteorological contexts it refers to small ice pellets formed when melted or partially melted snow refreezes in a subfreezing layer near the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are hailstorms?

options.A: Storms that produce only rain
options.B: Thunderstorms that produce hailstones, which grow in strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds by accretion of supercooled water

questions.explanation: Hailstorms are thunderstorms that produce hailstones, which grow in strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds by accretion of supercooled water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is precipitation measured?

options.A: Rainfall is measured using a barometer
options.B: Rainfall is measured using rain gauges, commonly reported in millimetres (mm), where 1 mm of rainfall equals 1 litre of water per square metre on a level surface, assuming no losses
options.C: Rainfall is measured using a thermometer
options.D: Rainfall is measured using an anemometer

questions.explanation: Rainfall is measured using rain gauges, commonly reported in millimetres (mm), where 1 mm of rainfall equals 1 litre of water per square metre on a level surface, assuming no losses.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a rain gauge?

options.A: An instrument that measures atmospheric pressure
options.B: An instrument that collects and measures liquid precipitation over a known area
options.C: An instrument that measures wind speed

questions.explanation: A rain gauge is an instrument that collects and measures liquid precipitation over a known area. Standard gauges may be non-recording or recording; tipping-bucket and weighing gauges provide time-resolved measurements.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an isohyet?

options.A: A line on a map joining places with equal temperature
options.B: A line on a map joining places with equal pressure
options.C: A line on a map joining places receiving equal amounts of precipitation over a specified period
options.D: A line on a map joining places with equal wind speed

questions.explanation: An isohyet is a line on a map joining places receiving equal amounts of precipitation over a specified period.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What factors affect rainfall distribution?

options.A: Only latitude
options.B: Latitude and global circulation; prevailing winds and moisture sources; distance from sea; mountain barriers and aspect; ocean currents; temperature and evaporation; air-mass and frontal activity; monsoon systems; and seasonal shifts of pressure belts

questions.explanation: Factors affecting rainfall distribution include latitude and global circulation; prevailing winds and moisture sources; distance from sea; mountain barriers and aspect; ocean currents; temperature and evaporation; air-mass and frontal activity; monsoon systems; and seasonal shifts of pressure belts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does the windward side of a mountain receive more rain?

options.A: The windward side is closer to the sun
options.B: Moist air is forced to rise, cool and condense on the windward slope; after losing moisture, descending air on the leeward side warms and its relative humidity decreases, reducing rainfall
options.C: The windward side has more vegetation
options.D: The windward side has higher pressure

questions.explanation: Moist air is forced to rise, cool and condense on the windward slope. After losing moisture, descending air on the leeward side warms and its relative humidity decreases, reducing rainfall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a rain shadow?

options.A: A region of heavy rainfall on the windward side
options.B: A relatively dry region on the leeward side of a mountain range, where descending air is warmer and drier after much of its moisture has been lost on the windward side

questions.explanation: A rain shadow is a relatively dry region on the leeward side of a mountain range, where descending air is warmer and drier after much of its moisture has been lost on the windward side.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the broad rainfall pattern in India?

options.A: Rainfall is evenly distributed throughout the year
options.B: Rainfall is strongly seasonal and spatially uneven; the southwest monsoon supplies most annual rainfall to much of India; very high totals occur in parts of the Western Ghats and northeast, while western Rajasthan and some rain-shadow interiors are much drier; Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share during the northeast monsoon
options.C: Rainfall is highest in western Rajasthan
options.D: Tamil Nadu receives most rainfall during the southwest monsoon

questions.explanation: Rainfall is strongly seasonal and spatially uneven. The southwest monsoon supplies most annual rainfall to much of India; very high totals occur in parts of the Western Ghats and northeast, while western Rajasthan and some rain-shadow interiors are much drier. Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share during the northeast monsoon.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between rainfall amount and rainfall intensity?

options.A: Amount is the rate of rainfall; intensity is the total depth
options.B: Amount is the total depth accumulated over a period; intensity is the rate of rainfall, often expressed in mm per hour
options.D: Amount is measured in mm/h; intensity is measured in mm

questions.explanation: Amount is the total depth accumulated over a period; intensity is the rate of rainfall, often expressed in mm per hour.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is weather?

options.A: The long-term statistical description of weather conditions
options.B: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, described by temperature, humidity, cloud, wind, pressure and precipitation

questions.explanation: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, described by temperature, humidity, cloud, wind, pressure and precipitation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is climate?

options.A: The short-term state of the atmosphere
options.B: The long-term statistical description of weather conditions and variability in a region, commonly assessed over a 30-year standard normal period
options.C: The daily temperature at a place
options.D: The wind speed at a place

questions.explanation: Climate is the long-term statistical description of weather conditions and variability in a region, commonly assessed over a 30-year standard normal period, although other periods may be used.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does weather differ from climate?

options.A: Weather describes long-term conditions; climate describes short-term conditions
options.B: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term averages, ranges, variability and probabilities of weather
options.D: Weather is measured in years; climate in days

questions.explanation: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term averages, ranges, variability and probabilities of weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main elements of climate?

options.A: Only temperature and rainfall
options.B: Temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity, cloud cover, sunshine and visibility

questions.explanation: The main elements of climate are temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity, cloud cover, sunshine and visibility.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major controls of climate?

options.A: Only latitude and altitude
options.B: Latitude; altitude; distance from sea and continentality; ocean currents; prevailing winds and air masses; pressure belts and global circulation; relief and aspect; vegetation and land cover; and human influences

questions.explanation: The major controls of climate include latitude; altitude; distance from sea and continentality; ocean currents; prevailing winds and air masses; pressure belts and global circulation; relief and aspect; vegetation and land cover; and human influences.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a climatic classification?

options.A: A list of weather events
options.B: A systematic grouping of world climates based on measurable characteristics such as temperature, precipitation, seasonality and vegetation
options.D: A description of a single climate

questions.explanation: A climatic classification is a systematic grouping of world climates based on measurable characteristics such as temperature, precipitation, seasonality and vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Koppen climate classification?

options.A: A classification based only on latitude
options.B: A widely used empirical climate classification developed by Wladimir Koppen, relating temperature and precipitation patterns to natural vegetation
options.C: A classification based only on ocean currents

questions.explanation: The Koppen climate classification is a widely used empirical climate classification developed by Wladimir Koppen, relating temperature and precipitation patterns to natural vegetation. Major groups are A tropical, B dry, C temperate, D continental/snow and E polar; highland climates are often treated separately or as a modifier.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group A represent?

options.A: Dry climates
options.B: Tropical climates where all months are warm; coldest-month mean generally ≥18°C

questions.explanation: Koppen group A represents tropical climates: all months warm; coldest-month mean generally ≥18°C. Subtypes include Af rainforest, Am monsoon and Aw/As savanna.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group B represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates where potential evaporation/evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation under classification criteria

questions.explanation: Koppen group B represents dry climates: potential evaporation/evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation under classification criteria. Subtypes include BW desert and BS steppe, with h hot and k cold variants.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group C represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates
options.C: Temperate climates with mild winters; coldest month below 18°C but above the D-group threshold

questions.explanation: Koppen group C represents temperate climates: mild winters; coldest month below 18°C but above the D-group threshold. Subtypes include Cf no dry season, Cw dry winter, Cs dry summer and a/b/c summer subtypes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group D represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates
options.D: Continental/snow climates with cold winters; coldest-month mean at or below about -3°C in the original/common threshold schemes; warmest month above 10°C

questions.explanation: Koppen group D represents continental/snow climates: cold winters; coldest-month mean at or below about -3°C in the original/common threshold schemes; warmest month above 10°C. Subtypes include Df, Dw, Ds and warm/cool summer subtypes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group E represent?

options.A: Tropical climates
options.B: Dry climates
options.D: Polar climates where the warmest month is below 10°C; subtypes ET tundra and EF ice cap

questions.explanation: Koppen group E represents polar climates: warmest month below 10°C. Subtypes include ET tundra and EF ice cap.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does Koppen group H represent?

options.A: Hot deserts
options.B: Highland climates controlled by altitude, often used as a supplementary category with strong local variation

questions.explanation: Koppen group H represents highland climates: altitude-controlled climates, often used as a supplementary category. Mountain climates with strong local variation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an equatorial climate?

options.A: A dry climate with very low rainfall
options.B: A hot, humid climate near the equator with small annual temperature range, high humidity and abundant rainfall in most months, often with frequent convectional thunderstorms; Koppen Af is tropical rainforest climate
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: An equatorial climate is a hot, humid climate near the equator with small annual temperature range, high humidity and abundant rainfall in most months, often with frequent convectional thunderstorms. Koppen Af is tropical rainforest climate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tropical monsoon climate?

options.A: A hot, humid climate with no dry season
options.B: A tropical climate with a pronounced wet season associated with monsoon circulation and a shorter dry season; Koppen Am has a short dry season but sufficient monsoon rainfall to maintain tropical vegetation
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A tropical monsoon climate is a tropical climate with a pronounced wet season associated with monsoon circulation and a shorter dry season. Koppen Am has a short dry season but sufficient monsoon rainfall to maintain tropical vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a savanna climate?

options.A: A hot, humid climate with no dry season
options.B: A tropical wet-and-dry climate with distinct rainy and dry seasons, generally supporting grassland with scattered trees; Koppen Aw or As depending on the dry season
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A savanna climate is a tropical wet-and-dry climate with distinct rainy and dry seasons, generally supporting grassland with scattered trees. Koppen Aw or As depending on the dry season.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a desert climate?

options.A: An arid climate where precipitation is very low relative to potential evapotranspiration; it may be hot (BWh) or cold (BWk); steppe climates (BS) are semi-arid
options.B: A hot, humid climate with abundant rainfall
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A desert climate is an arid climate where precipitation is very low relative to potential evapotranspiration. It may be hot (BWh) or cold (BWk); steppe climates (BS) are semi-arid.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a Mediterranean climate?

options.A: A climate with wet summers and dry winters
options.B: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters, commonly found on western sides of continents around 30°–45° latitude; Koppen Cs
options.C: A climate with rain all year and no seasonality
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A Mediterranean climate is a climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters, commonly found on western sides of continents around 30°–45° latitude. Koppen Cs.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a temperate climate?

options.A: A climate with extremely cold winters
options.B: A broad category with moderate temperatures compared with tropical and polar climates; in Koppen, C climates have mild winters and may be oceanic, humid subtropical or Mediterranean depending on precipitation and temperature seasonality
options.C: A climate with year-round high temperatures

questions.explanation: A temperate climate is a broad category with moderate temperatures compared with tropical and polar climates. In Koppen, C climates have mild winters and may be oceanic, humid subtropical or Mediterranean depending on precipitation and temperature seasonality.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a continental climate?

options.A: A climate with moderate temperatures and small annual range
options.B: A climate with large annual temperature range, commonly found in interiors and eastern parts of mid- to high-latitude continents, with cold winters and warm or hot summers; many correspond to Koppen D climates
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters
options.D: A polar climate with permanent ice

questions.explanation: A continental climate is a climate with large annual temperature range, commonly found in interiors and eastern parts of mid- to high-latitude continents, with cold winters and warm or hot summers. Many correspond to Koppen D climates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tundra climate?

options.A: A polar climate in which the warmest month is above 0°C but below 10°C; vegetation is low-growing and the growing season is short; Koppen ET
options.B: A climate with permanent ice and no vegetation
options.C: A hot, humid climate near the equator
options.D: A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wetter winters

questions.explanation: A tundra climate is a polar climate in which the warmest month is above 0°C but below 10°C; vegetation is low-growing and the growing season is short. Koppen ET.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an ice-cap climate?

options.A: A polar climate where the mean temperature of every month is below 0°C, preventing sustained tree or tundra vegetation; Koppen EF
options.B: A climate with warmest month above 10°C
options.C: A climate with hot, dry summers
options.D: A tropical climate with abundant rainfall

questions.explanation: An ice-cap climate is a polar climate where the mean temperature of every month is below 0°C, preventing sustained tree or tundra vegetation. Koppen EF.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a highland climate?

options.A: A climate with uniform temperature throughout the year
options.B: A climate strongly controlled by elevation, slope aspect and exposure; temperature generally decreases with altitude, while precipitation varies with relief and windward/leeward position
options.D: A climate found only at sea level

questions.explanation: A highland climate is a climate strongly controlled by elevation, slope aspect and exposure. Temperature generally decreases with altitude, while precipitation varies with relief and windward/leeward position.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the major climatic regions of the world?

options.A: Only tropical and polar regions
options.B: Equatorial rainforest; tropical monsoon; tropical savanna; hot and cold deserts/steppes; Mediterranean; humid subtropical; marine west coast/oceanic; humid continental; subarctic/taiga; tundra; ice-cap; and highland regions

questions.explanation: The major climatic regions of the world include equatorial rainforest; tropical monsoon; tropical savanna; hot and cold deserts/steppes; Mediterranean; humid subtropical; marine west coast/oceanic; humid continental; subarctic/taiga; tundra; ice-cap; and highland regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the limitations of the Koppen classification?

options.A: It is based entirely on wind patterns
options.B: It is empirical and uses thresholds that simplify gradual transitions; it does not fully represent microclimates, wind, extreme events, soil moisture or climate change, and boundaries may differ depending on dataset and normal period
options.D: It only applies to the Southern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: The Koppen classification is empirical and uses thresholds that simplify gradual transitions. It does not fully represent microclimates, wind, extreme events, soil moisture or climate change, and boundaries may differ depending on dataset and normal period.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does climate change affect climatic regions?

options.A: Climate change has no effect on climatic regions
options.B: Long-term warming and shifts in precipitation can move climatic boundaries, increase heat extremes and alter drought, snow and growing-season patterns; regional changes are not uniform
options.C: Climate change only affects polar regions
options.D: Climate change only affects ocean currents

questions.explanation: Long-term warming and shifts in precipitation can move climatic boundaries, increase heat extremes and alter drought, snow and growing-season patterns. Regional changes are not uniform.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a monsoon?

options.A: A daily reversal of wind direction
options.B: A seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds, accompanied by a distinct seasonal rainfall regime
options.C: A permanent wind blowing in one direction

questions.explanation: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds, accompanied by a distinct seasonal rainfall regime. The Indian monsoon is influenced by land-sea thermal contrast, seasonal migration of the ITCZ, pressure systems, topography, jet streams and ocean-atmosphere variability.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the origin of the Indian monsoon?

options.A: It results from a single factor: differential heating of land and sea
options.B: It results from interacting mechanisms: differential heating of the Asian landmass and Indian Ocean; seasonal northward shift of the ITCZ; development of low pressure over heated northwestern India and adjoining regions; cross-equatorial flow; Somali jet; Tibetan Plateau heating; and upper-air circulation changes
options.C: It is caused only by the Tibetan Plateau
options.D: It is caused only by ocean currents

questions.explanation: The Indian monsoon results from interacting mechanisms: differential heating of the Asian landmass and Indian Ocean; seasonal northward shift of the ITCZ; development of low pressure over heated northwestern India and adjoining regions; cross-equatorial flow; Somali jet; Tibetan Plateau heating; and upper-air circulation changes. No single-factor explanation is sufficient.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the southwest monsoon?

options.A: The winter monsoon from the northeast
options.B: The principal summer monsoon over India, generally arriving from the southwest from June and retreating progressively from September/October onward; it has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches and supplies most annual rainfall to much of the country
options.C: A local wind in southern India

questions.explanation: The southwest monsoon is the principal summer monsoon over India, generally arriving from the southwest from June and retreating progressively from September/October onward. It has Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches and supplies most annual rainfall to much of the country.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the northeast or retreating monsoon?

options.A: The principal summer monsoon over India
options.B: The seasonal flow from the northeast during the post-monsoon period, broadly October–December; it is generally dry for much of India but picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and brings important rainfall to Tamil Nadu and parts of the southeast coast
options.C: A local wind in northern India

questions.explanation: The northeast or retreating monsoon is the seasonal flow from the northeast during the post-monsoon period, broadly October–December. It is generally dry for much of India but picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and brings important rainfall to Tamil Nadu and parts of the southeast coast.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the two main branches of the southwest monsoon?

options.A: The Somali branch and the Tibetan branch
options.B: The Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch
options.C: The Western Ghats branch and the Himalayan branch
options.D: The northeast branch and the southeast branch

questions.explanation: The two main branches of the southwest monsoon are the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch. They interact with the Western Ghats, northeast India, the Himalaya and the monsoon trough.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Arabian Sea branch affect India?

options.A: It moves towards northeast India and the Ganga plains
options.B: It strikes the west coast and Western Ghats, producing heavy orographic rainfall on windward slopes; it also advances into central and northwestern India and contributes to rainfall over the peninsula
options.C: It brings rainfall only to Tamil Nadu
options.D: It has no effect on Indian rainfall

questions.explanation: The Arabian Sea branch strikes the west coast and Western Ghats, producing heavy orographic rainfall on windward slopes. It also advances into central and northwestern India and contributes to rainfall over the peninsula.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Bay of Bengal branch affect India?

options.A: It strikes the west coast and Western Ghats
options.B: It moves towards northeast India and the Ganga plains, often producing heavy rainfall over the northeast and Himalayan foothills; it then interacts with the monsoon trough and moves west/northwest across northern India
options.C: It brings rainfall only to Tamil Nadu
options.D: It has no effect on Indian rainfall

questions.explanation: The Bay of Bengal branch moves towards northeast India and the Ganga plains, often producing heavy rainfall over the northeast and Himalayan foothills. It then interacts with the monsoon trough and moves west/northwest across northern India.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the onset of monsoon?

options.A: The withdrawal of monsoon from a region
options.B: The arrival and establishment of sustained monsoon circulation and rainfall over a region; IMD declares onset over Kerala using defined large-scale circulation and rainfall criteria; onset dates vary from year to year
options.C: A temporary weakening of monsoon rainfall
options.D: A sudden increase in rainfall after onset

questions.explanation: The onset of monsoon is the arrival and establishment of sustained monsoon circulation and rainfall over a region. IMD declares onset over Kerala using defined large-scale circulation and rainfall criteria; onset dates vary from year to year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the normal onset period over Kerala?

options.A: Around 1 July
options.B: Around 1 June, but the actual date varies annually

questions.explanation: The long-term normal onset date used by IMD is around 1 June, but the actual date varies annually. It should not be treated as a fixed date.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the withdrawal of monsoon?

options.A: The arrival and establishment of sustained monsoon circulation
options.B: The progressive retreat of southwest monsoon circulation and rainfall, beginning generally from northwest India in September and spreading towards other regions; withdrawal dates vary by year
options.C: A temporary weakening of monsoon rainfall
options.D: A sudden increase in rainfall after onset

questions.explanation: The withdrawal of monsoon is the progressive retreat of southwest monsoon circulation and rainfall, beginning generally from northwest India in September and spreading towards other regions. Withdrawal dates vary by year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the burst of monsoon?

options.A: A temporary weakening of monsoon rainfall
options.B: A sudden increase in rainfall and the establishment of vigorous monsoon conditions after onset, often accompanied by widespread heavy rain; it is a descriptive term rather than a separate global circulation system
options.C: The withdrawal of monsoon from a region
options.D: The normal onset date over Kerala

questions.explanation: The burst of monsoon is a sudden increase in rainfall and the establishment of vigorous monsoon conditions after onset, often accompanied by widespread heavy rain. It is a descriptive term rather than a separate global circulation system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a break in monsoon?

options.A: A sudden increase in rainfall after onset
options.B: A temporary weakening or shift in monsoon rainfall over much of central India, often associated with a northward displacement of the monsoon trough towards the Himalayan foothills; rain may continue or intensify in Himalayan foothill and northeast regions
options.C: The withdrawal of monsoon from a region
options.D: The normal onset date over Kerala

questions.explanation: A break in monsoon is a temporary weakening or shift in monsoon rainfall over much of central India, often associated with a northward displacement of the monsoon trough towards the Himalayan foothills. Rain may continue or intensify in Himalayan foothill and northeast regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the monsoon trough?

options.A: A high-pressure zone over the Indian Ocean
options.B: An elongated low-pressure zone extending across northern India during the southwest monsoon, often linking heat low regions in the west with low-pressure systems over the Bay of Bengal; its position influences rainfall distribution
options.D: A wind pattern in southern India

questions.explanation: The monsoon trough is an elongated low-pressure zone extending across northern India during the southwest monsoon, often linking heat low regions in the west with low-pressure systems over the Bay of Bengal. Its position influences rainfall distribution.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are western disturbances?

options.A: Local winds in western India
options.B: Eastward-moving extratropical weather systems originating or developing over the Mediterranean-West Asian region and travelling towards South Asia; they bring winter rain to northwest India and snowfall in the western Himalaya, and can interact with monsoon systems
options.C: Tropical cyclones in the Arabian Sea

questions.explanation: Western disturbances are eastward-moving extratropical weather systems originating or developing over the Mediterranean-West Asian region and travelling towards South Asia. They bring winter rain to northwest India and snowfall in the western Himalaya, and can interact with monsoon systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is El Nino?

options.A: A periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific
options.B: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific associated with weakening of the normal Walker circulation; it can alter global rainfall and temperature patterns and is often associated with a weaker Indian summer monsoon, but the relationship is not deterministic
options.C: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: El Nino is a periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific associated with weakening of the normal Walker circulation. It can alter global rainfall and temperature patterns and is often associated with a weaker Indian summer monsoon, but the relationship is not deterministic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is La Nina?

options.A: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific
options.B: A periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, generally associated with stronger-than-normal trade winds and Walker circulation; it often favours a stronger Indian monsoon, but other factors can modify the outcome
options.C: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: La Nina is a periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, generally associated with stronger-than-normal trade winds and Walker circulation. It often favours a stronger Indian monsoon, but other factors can modify the outcome.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Southern Oscillation?

options.A: A periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific
options.B: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific, commonly monitored using pressure differences such as the Tahiti-Darwin index; it is the atmospheric component of ENSO
options.C: A periodic cooling of the equatorial Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Southern Oscillation is a seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and central/eastern tropical Pacific, commonly monitored using pressure differences such as the Tahiti-Darwin index. It is the atmospheric component of ENSO.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is ENSO?

options.A: A type of monsoon wind
options.B: The El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon involving sea-surface temperature changes in the equatorial Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation
options.C: A local wind in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: ENSO is the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon involving sea-surface temperature changes in the equatorial Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)?

options.A: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and eastern Pacific
options.B: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern involving differences in sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean; a positive IOD often supports Indian monsoon rainfall, but its influence varies and interacts with ENSO
options.C: A periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific
options.D: A local wind in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is a coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern involving differences in sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean. A positive IOD often supports Indian monsoon rainfall, but its influence varies and interacts with ENSO.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO)?

options.A: A periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific
options.B: A large-scale eastward-moving pulse of enhanced and suppressed tropical convection and circulation, typically recurring on intraseasonal timescales of roughly 30–60 days; its phase can modulate monsoon active and break spells
options.C: A seesaw in atmospheric pressure between the western and eastern Pacific
options.D: A coupled ocean-atmosphere pattern in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is a large-scale eastward-moving pulse of enhanced and suppressed tropical convection and circulation, typically recurring on intraseasonal timescales of roughly 30–60 days. Its phase can modulate monsoon active and break spells.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the monsoon affect Indian agriculture?

options.A: It has no effect on agriculture
options.B: It supplies water for rain-fed crops, reservoirs and groundwater recharge; delayed onset, long breaks, uneven distribution or excess rainfall affect sowing, crop growth, yields, irrigation demand and rural livelihoods

questions.explanation: The monsoon supplies water for rain-fed crops, reservoirs and groundwater recharge. Delayed onset, long breaks, uneven distribution or excess rainfall affect sowing, crop growth, yields, irrigation demand and rural livelihoods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is monsoon variability?

options.A: The permanent constancy of monsoon rainfall
options.B: Variability in onset, withdrawal, total rainfall, spatial distribution, intensity and active/break spells across years and within a season; it is influenced by ENSO, IOD, MJO, land-atmosphere feedbacks, circulation and regional factors
options.C: The daily change in monsoon winds
options.D: The seasonal reversal of winds only

questions.explanation: Monsoon variability is variability in onset, withdrawal, total rainfall, spatial distribution, intensity and active/break spells across years and within a season. It is influenced by ENSO, IOD, MJO, land-atmosphere feedbacks, circulation and regional factors.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are drought conditions?

options.A: A situation where water overflows normally dry land
options.B: A prolonged period of deficient precipitation or water availability relative to normal, causing meteorological, agricultural, hydrological or socioeconomic impacts; drought definitions depend on the type and region

questions.explanation: Drought conditions are a prolonged period of deficient precipitation or water availability relative to normal, causing meteorological, agricultural, hydrological or socioeconomic impacts. Drought definitions depend on the type and region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are flood conditions?

options.A: A prolonged period of deficient precipitation
options.B: A situation where water overflows normally dry land or river channels exceed their capacity; floods can result from intense rainfall, prolonged monsoon rain, cyclones, storm surge, snowmelt, dam releases or poor drainage

questions.explanation: Flood conditions are a situation where water overflows normally dry land or river channels exceed their capacity. Floods can result from intense rainfall, prolonged monsoon rain, cyclones, storm surge, snowmelt, dam releases or poor drainage.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why can a strong monsoon still produce drought in some areas and floods in others?

options.A: Because strong monsoons always produce uniform rainfall
options.B: Because seasonal total rainfall can be unevenly distributed; persistent breaks, localised cloudbursts, terrain, drainage, soil moisture and reservoir operations can create contrasting impacts over short distances
options.C: Because drought and floods cannot occur in the same season
options.D: Because monsoon rainfall is always predictable

questions.explanation: Seasonal total rainfall can be unevenly distributed. Persistent breaks, localised cloudbursts, terrain, drainage, soil moisture and reservoir operations can create contrasting impacts over short distances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Western Ghats influence monsoon rainfall?

options.A: The Ghats have no effect on monsoon rainfall
options.B: The Ghats force moist Arabian Sea air to rise, causing heavy windward rainfall; the leeward Deccan interior receives less orographic rainfall and includes rain-shadow areas
options.C: The Ghats cause the leeward side to receive heavy rainfall
options.D: The Ghats block all monsoon rainfall

questions.explanation: The Ghats force moist Arabian Sea air to rise, causing heavy windward rainfall. The leeward Deccan interior receives less orographic rainfall and includes rain-shadow areas.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of the Tibetan Plateau in the monsoon system?

options.A: It has no role in the monsoon system
options.B: Its elevated land surface influences upper-air heating and circulation during the warm season and is one component of the broader Asian monsoon system
options.C: It blocks monsoon winds from reaching India
options.D: It causes the monsoon to occur in winter

questions.explanation: The Tibetan Plateau's elevated land surface influences upper-air heating and circulation during the warm season and is one component of the broader Asian monsoon system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a cyclone?

options.A: A large-scale high-pressure system
options.B: A large-scale low-pressure system with winds spiralling inward near the surface; in the Northern Hemisphere the circulation is generally anticlockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere it is generally clockwise, due to the Coriolis effect

questions.explanation: A cyclone is a large-scale low-pressure system with winds spiralling inward near the surface. In the Northern Hemisphere the circulation is generally anticlockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere it is generally clockwise, due to the Coriolis effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main types of cyclones?

options.A: Only tropical cyclones
options.B: Tropical cyclones, extratropical or temperate cyclones, and smaller-scale phenomena such as tornadoes; their energy sources and structures differ

questions.explanation: The main types of cyclones are tropical cyclones, extratropical or temperate cyclones, and smaller-scale phenomena such as tornadoes. Their energy sources and structures differ.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a tropical cyclone?

options.A: A cold-core, frontal, organised low-pressure system
options.B: A warm-core, non-frontal, organised low-pressure system developing over sufficiently warm tropical or subtropical oceans, with deep convection and a closed low-level circulation
options.C: A high-pressure system with sinking air
options.D: A local wind caused by terrain

questions.explanation: A tropical cyclone is a warm-core, non-frontal, organised low-pressure system developing over sufficiently warm tropical or subtropical oceans, with deep convection and a closed low-level circulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What conditions favour tropical cyclone formation?

options.A: Cold ocean water and high vertical wind shear
options.B: Warm ocean water generally at least about 26.5°C over a sufficient depth; abundant moisture; atmospheric instability; low vertical wind shear; a pre-existing disturbance and low-level convergence; and sufficient Coriolis force, so formation is uncommon very near the equator
options.D: Strong vertical wind shear and cold ocean water

questions.explanation: Conditions favouring tropical cyclone formation include warm ocean water, generally at least about 26.5°C over a sufficient depth; abundant moisture; atmospheric instability; low vertical wind shear; a pre-existing disturbance and low-level convergence; and sufficient Coriolis force, so formation is uncommon very near the equator.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does a tropical cyclone form?

options.A: Cold air sinks and forms a low-pressure system
options.B: A pre-existing tropical disturbance gathers warm, moist air; condensation releases latent heat, warming the core and lowering pressure; surface air converges and rises; the Coriolis force organises rotation; if environmental conditions remain favourable, the system can intensify
options.C: A front forms between two air masses
options.D: A high-pressure system develops over land

questions.explanation: A pre-existing tropical disturbance gathers warm, moist air. Condensation releases latent heat, warming the core and lowering pressure. Surface air converges and rises; the Coriolis force organises rotation. If environmental conditions remain favourable, the system can intensify.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the structure of a mature tropical cyclone?

options.A: A uniform layer of clouds with no distinct features
options.B: A central eye (in intense systems), surrounding eyewall with strongest winds and intense rainfall, and spiral rainbands extending outward; it has a warm core and a deep circulation
options.C: A cold core with frontal boundaries
options.D: A high-pressure centre with sinking air
